Hunter Aircrafts 
*323. SHRI C. M. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the 'Hunter' a veteran aircraft of 1971 Indo-Pak War, made its last 
flight at the Air Force Day Parade 2001; 
(b) if so, how many Hunters had been grounded that day; and 
(c) the aircraft that is expected to take over the role of the 'Hunter' in the 
Air Force Fleet? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERN ANDES): (a) to 
(c) The Hunter aircraft made its last flight on 8th October, 2001 (Air Force 
Day) when it was ceremoniously phased out during the Air Force Day 
Parade at the Air Force Station, Palam. 
A total of eight Hunter air crafts were phased out on 8th October, 2001. With 
that all Hunter aircrafts were phased out of service. 
Another suitable aircraft has been assigned the role of Hunter in the Indian 
Air Force. However, details cannot be divulged due to reasons of national 
security. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA       [12 December, 2001] 
Activities of Lashkar-e-Toiba in India 
*324. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it has come to the Government's notice that Pakistan-based terrorist 
organisation, Lashkar-e-Toiba (L-e-T) is functioning in more than 36 cities in India, 
backing organised criminal gangs and is involved in large scale drug trafficking and 
smuggling of counterfeit Indian currency; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what steps have been taken so far to smash the disruptive activities of 
L-e-T and similar terrorist outfits operating in this country and with what 
results? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) and (b) Lashkar-e-
Toiba is mainly operating in Jammu and Kashmir, but there are reports that the 
outfit has spread its network in other parts of the country as well like 
Hyderabad, Mumbai, Jodhpur, Kanpur, Dehradun, Bhuj and Delhi. No confirmed 
report of LeT's involvement in drug trafficking and smuggling of counterfeit Indian 
currency has been received. However, such possibilities cannot be ruled out. 
(c) Government has adopted a well coordinated and multi-pronged approach for 
tackling the activities of militants which includes strengthening the border 
management to check illegal cross border activities, gearing up the intelligence 
machinery, close interaction between agencies of the Centre and the State 
Governments, neutralizing plans of militants and anti-national elements by 
coordinated action, modernization and upgradation of police and security forces 
with advanced sophisticated weapons and communication system, etc. As a 
result of coordinated action, several terrorist modules have been neutralized. 
Diplomatic initiatives have also been taken with various countries to enlist 
their support in countering the activities of militant groups. 
6 

[12 December, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance, 2001 has been promulgated under 
which 25 organisations, including Lashkar-e-Toiba have been notified as 
Terrorist Organisations.

IPS Officer held in Dowry Case 
*331. SHRI KHAGEN DAS: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
titled "IPS officer held for demanding Rs. 5 crore dowry" appearing in the

(b) whether the alleged officer has since been suspended from 
11 

RAJYA SABHA       [12 December, 2001] 
service; and 
(c) what steps have been taken to ensure that the officer does not use his 
influence in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The IPS officer in question , who belongs to Madhya Pradesh cadre,

State Government of Madhya Pradesh is competent to proceed against the officer 
since he is presently serving in connection with the affairs of that State. It is also 
for the State Government to ensure that the officer is not able to influence or 
interfere with the investigation of the case.

Naval Base Project Seabird, Karnataka 
*334. SHRI K.V. KRISHNAMURTHY:  Will the Minister of DEFENCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the new naval base Project Seabird near Karwar (Karnataka) 
was envisaged in the Naval Plan 1980—55 to be completed by 1995; 
(b) whether the original project outlay of  Rs. 350 crore in 1985 escalated 
to Rs. 1295 crore in 1995, despite reduction in scope by more than 50 per 
cent; and 
(c) whether the rehabilitation package fo r the displaced families is in 
place and if so, when the project is likely to be commissioned? 
14 

[12 December, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERN ANDES): (a) to 
(c) In August 1985 the Ministry of Defence approved the construction of a 
Naval Base at Karwar at an initial estimated expenditure of Rs. 350.00 crores. 
The initial estimates were indicative and were made without a Master Plan 
and a Detailed Project Report. The scope of work, different Sub components 
of the Dockyard and details regarding supporting Infrastructure had not been 
worked out. In the year 1989 a Consultant was appointed to draw the Master 
Plan and detailed Project report for Phase-1-A and 1-B of the Project. The 
Consultant submitted his report in 1990. However, the Project could not 
progress further due to financial constraints. Based on the Final Project 
Report, with reduced scope of Phase-I, when compared with the initial 
proposal and keeping in view the escalation of price level in the meantime, the 
Ministry of Defence finally approved in October 1995 the construction of 
Phase-I of the Project at a projected cost of Rs. 1294.41 crores. 
The rehabilitation package finalized  in consultation with the State 
Government, included interalia, a cash allowance and a house site, education 
stipend, and relief for food and medicines. The rehabilitation Project has 
been finalized at a total amount of Rs. 126.96 crores and State Government 
of Karnataka has already been paid a sum of Rs. 117.02 crores. The Balance 
amount will be paid on Audit of accounts. 
The Project is scheduled to be completed by 2005.

2446. DR. KARAN SINGH: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be

(c) what were the precise functions of TA as envisaged at that time; and 
how far they have been watered down? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. Territorial Army (TA) and some units of Navy and Air Force 
similar to TA were in existence at 
45 

RAJYA SABHA       [12 December, 2001] 
the time of Independence. In 1949, the projected strength of the Territorial 
Army alone was 1.3 lakhs. Over the years, the territorial equivalents of the 
Navy and Air Force have ceased to exist and some of the Territorial Army 
units have been converted to regular army units. The current strength of the 
Territorial Army stands at 32,200 personnel. 
(c) The role and function of Territorial Army, in 1951, included: (i) 
relieve the regular army of static duties; (ii) provide coastal defence 
and anti-aircraft units; (iii) provide field formations and units for the 
regular army, as and when required. 
These functions have undergone certain modifications over the years to 
suit the changinng internal and external security environment. The present 
functions of the force include carrying out static security duties, internal 
security duties and aid to civil authorities, as and when required.

2473. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER  DAVE: Will the Minister of

64 

[12 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) to 
(d) The Following arrangements exist for giving warning signals to 
fishermen: 
(i) Weather bulletins including cyclone warning for fishermen are 
broadcast on AIR. 
(ii) Storm warning signals in the form of flags/lights are displayed at 
all ports. 
(iii) Related State Government Departments are informed of impending 
danger at sea so that they can also inform the fishermen. 
(iv) In addition, regular instructional lectures are organised by Coast Guard to 
indicate maritime boundaries and safety precautions. 
Fishermen being apprehended by Pakistan cannot be attributed to failure on the 
Part of Coast Guard as despite advice they do not keep within national maritime 
boundaries. It has been found that fishermen's boats are not properly equipped 
with communication and navigational equipment. In addition, some fishermen 
continue to disregard the advice given by Coast Guard and get apprehended by 
Pakistan Maritime Security Agency (MSA). 
Fishing in territorial waters (Up to 12 nautical mile) is a state subject and 
the operations of fishermen are governed by Marine Fisheries Regulation Act of 
the respective coastal states. The Un ion Government is responsible for 
administering operations of fishermen in deep sea (beyond 12 nautical miles and 
up to 200 nautical miles). 
Coast Guard has recommended to State Governments to equip fishing vessels 
with basic radio communication equipment. The Union Ministry of Agriculture is 
examining a proposal of establishing satellite based Vessel Management 
System for fishing vessels.

Pakistani National Getting Indian Identity Proofs 
2508. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have prepared an action plan to keep a watch on the 
large number of Pakistani Nationals, who visits the country on short term basis 
and later acquire Indian identity by acquiring ration cards and passports and are 
helping anti-national elements; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to be taken by Government to tighten the 
verification system for issue of driving license, identity cards etc. so that 
foreigners are not able to assume a local identity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) to (c) In order to 
keep a close watch on the Pak Nationals visiting India on short-term visa, the 
following procedure has been prescribed: 
1. The visa applications are received in quadruplicate; 
2. The visa is given for a specified city/town and the visa holder is not 
allowed to visit any other place without seeking prior permission; 
3. One copy of the application form is given to the visa holder, one is 
retained by the Mission, one is sent to the Superintendent of Police of the 
first place to be visited by the visa holder and one copy is sent to the 
Revenue Intelligence; 
94 

[12 December, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
4. The visa holder hands over his copy of the application to the Immigration 
Officer at the checkpost of entry; 
5. A temporary permit is issued to him (if his stay is more than 14 days) and 
copies of this are sent to all the Superintendents of Police of the places to 
be visited by the Pak visa holder; 
6. Pak visa holder is required to report to the SP of the place of his first visit 
and subsequent places of visit within 24 hrs where he is given a regular 
residential permit specifying the permitted period of his stay. The Pak visa 
holder is required to intimate his intended departure to another place in 
India/return to his country to the SP 24 hrs in advance; 
7. The check-post of entry and exit and the mode of his travel are also 
specified on the visa and he has to seek permission for change in any of 
these. The check post of exit, if it is different from the checkpost of entry, 
informs the check-post of entry about the departure of the visa holder. 
Thus, all efforts are made to ensure that the Pak Nationals coming to the 
country on short-term visa go back to their country. Such of them who do not 
abide by the terms and conditions of visa are dealt with under the Foreigners Act 
for which powers have been delegated to the State Governments. The names of 
such nationals are put on the negative list. 
Driving licenses, ration cards, etc. are issued by the State Govts, after local 
verification of the particulars furnished by the applicant through the State police 
authorities. If a foreigner manages to acquire any of these documents by 
misrepresentation of facts, action is taken against him and he is deported back to his 
country for which powers have been delegated to the State Governments. The 
State Governments are regularly sensitised on the need to carefully scrutinize 
and verify all applications before issue of such documents.

2542. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether with a view to prioritizing hydro-electric power projects for 
speedy implementation basin-wise ranking studies have been carried out by the 
Central Electricity Authority; 
(b) if so, the details of the hydro-projects identified for prioritization, 
basin-wise; the power potential of each and the cost thereof; and 
(c) whether any new projects have been identified in the Krishna, Godavari and 
Cauveri basins, Bhima and Seena river basins, if so, the time frame 
contemplated for implementing the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Government of India is 
according high priority to exploit the untapped hydro-electric potential in the 
country. In order to accelerate the process of survey and investigation of the new 
hydroelectric sites and to create a shelf of feasible projects which could be taken up 
for execution, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) was asked to carry out a 
ranking study of the balance hydro sites for all the six river basins classified in 
the country. CEA has since brought out a Report on Preliminary Ranking Study 
of about 400 hydro schemes with an aggregate installed capacity of about 
1,07,000 MW which were identified but are yet to be developed. The inter-se-
prioritization of hydro sites within the basins has been carried out on

Steps for Making SGSY more Effective 
2546. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the objective of the Swamajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY); 
(b) whether these objectives have been fulfilled till date; 
(c) if so, the number of employment provided to the rural population 
through this scheme till date; and 
(d) the details of steps being taken to make this scheme more effective and 
productive? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) The objective of the Swamajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana 
(SGSY) is to bring the assisted poor families (swarozgaris) above the poverty line 
in three yean by providing them income-generating assets through a mix of 
bank credit and government subsidy. The assisted families, may be individuals 
or groups (Self Help Groups). However, the emphasis under the Scheme will 
be on Group Approach. 
(b) The SGSY is an on-going and process oriented Scheme. It may 
be, therefore, too early to say that  objectives of the Scheme have 
been fulfilled. The fact that 6.S8  lakhs Self Help Groups (SGHs) 
have been formed all over the Country, since inception of the 
Scheme, shows that the Scheme is progressing satisfactorily and on 
expected lines. 
(c) Since inception of the Scheme, till date, 22.76 lakhs 
Swarozgaries have been assisted fo r various economic activities with a 
total investment of Rs. 4290.79 Crores, involving Rs. 1424.19 Crores, 
as Subsidy and Rs. 2866.60 Crores as Credit from Banks. 
(d) Various steps being taken by the Ministry to make this Scheme 
more effective and productive includes, regular sensitisation of 
District and Field level functionaries and bankers, promotion of 
marketing of the SGSY products by participating in State, National 
and International exhibitions, regular inspection and verification of 
168 

[12 December, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
the Assets by Area officers under the Area officers Scheme, monitoring of the 
progress through Monthly, Quarterly, Half-yearly and Annual Periodical Reports, 
review of the Scheme by the Central level Coordination Committee and 
Performance Review Committee, Evaluation studies through reputed 
institutions/organisations, concurrent evaluations etc. An important step taken in 
this regard recently was holding of the National Conference on "Self Help 
Group Movement in the Country and the SGSY" at National Institute of 
Rural Development (NIRD), Hyderabad. The participants in the Conference 
included several Chief Ministers, Ministers of Rural Development from States, 
Senior Officials from Reserve Bank of India, NABARD, concerned 
Ministries, Departments and other agencies.

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (c) Under the 
Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP), funds are not allocated to the States, but 
are released to the Programme districts on project to project basis. A watershed 
development project taken up under the programme is required to be completed 
over a period of five years and funds are released for its completion in seven 
instalments. The first instalment is released along with the sanction of the project. 
Thereafter, each subsequent instalment is released on receipt of specific proposal

instalment is ensured at the time of release of subsequent instalment. Statement

structures, renovation of wells, gully control structures, diversion bunds, water 
delivery channels, contour bunding, road side plantation, tree plantation, live 
fencing, kitchen garden package, mango plantation, cashew plantation, mushroom 
cultivation, pasture development, etc.

New Scheme for total poverty-alleviation 
†2551. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: WiU the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any new ambitions scheme for 
total proverty alleviation; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) and (b) An ambitious Scheme namely the Sampooma Grameen 
Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) has been launched w.e.f. 25th September, 2001 to 
create additional wage employment with food security in the rural areas. 
There is, however, no scheme in the Ministry of Rural Development for total 
poverty alleviation. 
As regards the Sampooma Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY), the 
Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) and the jawahar Gram Samridhi 
Yojana (JGSY) will get fully merged with the new Scheme. However, the 
EAS and JGSY will continue as a part of the new Scheme for the current 
year. Under the SGRY, 50 lakh tonnes of foodgrains amounting to Rs. 5000 
crores (at economic cost) will be provided every year, free of cost to the State 
Governments and Union Territory Administrations. The remaining funds 
(Rs. 5000 crores) will be utilized, to meet the cash component of wages and 
material cost. About 100 crores mandays of employment are envisaged to be 
generated every year in the rural areas through the SGRY.

Land Reforms as policy Instrument for Alleviation of Rural Poverty 
2563. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Ninth Plan identified the land reforms as an 
important policy instrument for the alleviation of rural poverty; 
(b) if so, the progress report of the various States in this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the Planning Commission has expressed unhappiness 
over the lack of progress in this regard in the midterm plan appraisal; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government and action proposed to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (d) The 
schemes/activities undertaken towards land reforms have. br ought about a 
significant change in agrarian structure. 92% of the holdings in the country are now 
wholly-owned and self-operative. Ownership rights have been granted to 20 
million tillers and S.31 million acres of ceiling surplus land have been distributed 
to S.S4 million rural poor. Moreover, 14.75 million acres of Government 
Wastelands and 2.18 million acres of Bhoodanland have also been distributed 
among the eligible rural poor. 12.42 million tenants have their rights protected over 
an area of 15.63 million acres of land and 0.43 million acres of alienated land has 
been restored to STs. The Scheme of Computerisation of Land Records is being 
implemented in 569 districts of the country. 
The Planning Commission in its mid-term plan appraisal had observed that 
several factors had constrained the progress of Computerisation of Land Records 
such as delay in transfer of funds to the implementing authority by the State 
Governments, power shortages and delay in the construction of room with air 
conditioner for installation of computers and other equipments, delay in 
development of appropriate and comprehensive software as per requirement   of   
the   State   Governments,   delay   in   supply   and 
201 

RAJYA SABHA      [12 December, 2001] 
installation of the hardware, lack of adequate training facilities to staff to 
handle computers and non-availability of good vendors for taking up data 
entry work. 
With a view to speeding up the progress of the Scheme of 
Computerisation of Land Records, th e State Govts./UTs were impressed 
upon to take effective steps for tran sfer of funds to the implementing 
agencies in time and also to take up data entry work through private vendors 
so that the work could be completed within a specified time-frame. The State 
Govts /UTs have also been requested to procure and install hardware at the 
earliest and organise basic training programmes in order to train the Revenue 
Officials at the taluk level to facilitate speedy implementation of the Scheme.

Importing clothes on the basis of Export Quota by the US 
† 2569. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
                  SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN':  
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that even today the US is importing clothes on the 
basis of export quota fixed for the countries; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that the quota system has been causing a lot 
of hindrances in liberalisation policy of industry; and 
(c) if so, the reaction of Government  thereto and whether Government 
have urged upon the US to' do away with quota-system? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) to (c) Textile imports in USA are governed by 
bilateral textile agreements entered into between India and other countries under the 
aegis of the Multi-Fibre Arrangement (MFA) which has since 1.1.1995, become 
part of the Agreement on Textiles & Clothing (ATC) contained in the Final Act of 
the Uruguay Round negotiations of the GATT. Quotas by themselves are trade 
restrictive. 
As per ATC, the textile quotas wo uld be phased out by 1st January 
2005.

2570. SHRI BRATIN SENGUP TA: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) Whether the working group on Textiles and Jute Industry has recommended 
a uniform 8 per cent excise duty for the entire textile sector for next five years as 
a special dispensation; 
(b) If so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) Whether the total textile imports during the last fiscal year has increased 
substantially, but the exports were not increasing at the   • same rate; and 
(d) If so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAY KUMAR) (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Working Group on 
Textile and Jute Industry for 10th Five Year Plan (2002—07) has recommended a 
number of measures to promote and develop the Indian Textile Industry for 
consideration of the Planning Commission. One of them is to broaden the tax 
net to link all states of textile production i.e. from fiber to the fabric stage by 
reducing the excise duty structure to a uniform level of 8 per cent.

year as against a decline of 25.2 per cent in total textile imports, in value

adequate availability of yarn packed in hank form for use in handlooms;

handloom sector to cope with the competition from other sectors.

FatalAccidents on National Highways 
*342. PROF. A. LAKSHMISAGAR: 
SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: 
Will the Minister of ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS bepleasedto 
state: 
(a) whether Government have made any assessment of the fatal road 
accidents on the country's highways a nd the percentage by which such 
accidents have risen during the last three years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, year-wise; 
(c) whether Government have critically evaluated the factors responsible 
for the rising number of such fatal road accidents besides examining the highways 
designs; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the measures contemplated by Government to make the National 
Highways more safe ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD TRANSPORT 
AND HIGHWAYS [(MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDUPJ)]: (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
The data on road accidents on the Na tional Highways are collected annually 
from the States. As per information available, for the years 1998, 1999 and 2000 
the percentage rise in number of fatalities on National Highways each year has 
been about 3.2%. 4.5%and 3.8% respectively. The data for years 1998,1999 and 
2000 are provisional and as such percentage increase are also provisional. 
(c) and (d) analysis of the various road accidents attributes the causes of 
road accidents to drivers, pedestrians/passengers, mechanical defects in motor 
vehicles, bad weather, condition of roads and other causes. 
(e) Necessary measures of road Sa fety on all National Highways are 
incorporated in the Road Design at the detailed project report stage for the 
concerned National Highways. The Government is taking a number of steps 
besides highway design to improve the road safety on National Highways. 
These include: 
(i) Giving grant-in-aid to voluntary organizations for administering 
road safety programmes in order to create awareness among the 
public. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [13 December. 2001] 
(ii) Refresher training of Heavy Motor Vehicle Drivers and use of 
driving'simulators. 
(iii) Publicity campaign on Road Safety Awareness through audio-
visual-print media. 
(iv) National Award has been instituted for voluntary organizations/ 
individuals for outstanding work in the field of road safety. 
(v) All India Essay Competition on road safety are organizaed for 
school children for creating awareness among the school children. 
(vi) Observance of Road Safety Week in the first week of every year 
across the country. 
(vii) Annual fitness certificate of commercial vehicles is necessary as 
per provision of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 
(viii) Introduction of Smart Card, based driving licenses. 
(ix) Transport Minister's Trophy for State Transport Undertakings 
having lowest accident record, etc. 
(x) Provision of cranes and ambulances under National Highway 
Accident Relief Service Scheme to States/NGOs, etc. 
(xi) Road Patrolling on a part of National Highways-8 has been taken 
up as an experimental measure. 
Labour Reforms 
*343. SHRI SURESH PA CHOURI: Will the Minist er of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to introduce labour reforms in the country; 
(b) if so, the details; and 
(c) the reasons for delay in introducin g labour reforms in the wake of 
introduction of structural reforms since 1991 ? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SHARAD YADAV) : (a) to (c) 
Review/updation of labour laws is a continuous process in order to bring them 
in tune with the prevailing situation and emerging needs of the economy. Taking 
into consideration the requirement of productivity, competitiveness and 
employment generation and to update the provisions, especially since the 
introduction of economic reforms beginning 1991. need has been felt from time 
4 

[13 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
lo time to make amendments in certain labour legislations and steps initiated 
accordingly. A Group of Ministers on Labour Reforms has been constituted. 
The Government has also set up the Second National Commission on 
Labour with a view to suggest rationalization of existing laws relating to labour 
in die organised sector and to suggest an umbrella legislation for ensuring a 
minimum level of protection to the workers in the unorganized sector. The 
Commission would, inter-alia, take into account th e emerging economic 
environment involving rapid technological changes, globalisation of economy, 
liberalization of trade and industry, emphasis on international competitiveness 
and also the need for bringing the existing laws in tune with the future labour 
market needs and demands. The report of the Commission is expected by 15-
02-2002.

Central Assistance to States 
*347. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRL A: 
SHRI AN ANTRA Y DEVSHANKER DAVE:  
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Planning Commission have decided to review the 
Gadgil-Mukherjee formula for allocation of Central Assistance to States; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether several Slates are unhappy on the allocation of Central 
Assistance due to Gadgil-Mukherjee formula; and 
(d) if so, the details of representations received in this regard and further 
action taken thereon ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRTMATIVASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (d) The Planning Commission has 
received proposals from various State Governments to amend the existing Gadgil 
formula for allocating Normal Central Assistance to State Plans. There is wide 
divergence in the views amongst the States in this regard- In general, while the 
advanced States have sought higher weightage for performance, the less 
advanced States have sought higher weightage for backwardness. This issue 
was considered in a meeting of the Full Planning Commission held on 27th and 
29th June 2001. Since revision in the Formula requires the approval of National 
Development Council (NDC), it was decided that given the difference of opinion 
among the State Governments and the sensitivity of this issue, it was necessary 
to discuss this further and evolve a consensus before alternatives are considered 
by the NDC. 
Ceiling on bonus 
*348. SHRI JIBON ROY : Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that upper ceiling of the guaranteed bonus for the 
industrial workers has not been changed since last decades; 
(b) the details of the upper ceiling stipulated when the Bonus Act was 
passed with corresponding Consumer Price Index and the current upper ceiling 
with the corresponding Consumer Price Index; and 
7 

RAJYASABHA [13 December,2001] 
(c) the steps taken by Government to withdraw upper ceiling on payment 
of bonus ? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRISHARAD YAD AV) : (a) to (c) The 
Payment of Bonus Act was enacted in 1965. Originally the Act provided for an 
eligibility limit of Rs. 1600 p.m. of wages and calculation ceiling of Rs. 750 p.m. 
which were raised to Rs. 2500 and Rs. 1600 respectively in 1985 (w.e.f. 7-11-85). 
The ceilings were subsequently raised to Rs. 3500 and Rs. 2500 respectively in 
1995, effective 1 -4-93. The Consumer Price Index Numbers for Industrial Workers 
(base 1960 = 100) for the year 1965 was 132 and for 1985, it was 625. The index as 
on 1 -4-93 with new CPI base (1982) was 243 which when converted to 1960 base 
comes to 1198. The latest CPI at 1982 base is 468 for the month of October, 2001 
which works out to 2307 at 1960 base. 
The Government is seized of the demand regarding the amendment of 
Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 for raising the eligibility and calculation ceilings. 
The issue is under examination in the light of its wide ranging repercussions as 
the benefits of bonus will have to be extended to, besides the Private Sector, to 
the employees of PSUs (both Central and States), Central and State Governments 
and autonomous organizations resulting in huge financial burden to the 
Government exchequer.

India's Stand on Afghan War 
2653. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHAR YA : Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Osama bin Laden and the Talibans were being patronised 
and encouraged by some advanced developed countries to subserve into own 
national interest for a long lime: 
(b) if so, whether the same country could be morally capable of fighting 
out the menace globally. 
(c) if so. whether Indian Governments response to the Afghan war should 
be ascertained accordingly: and 
(d) if so. what is the present situation in respect to our role globally? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASW ANT SINGH): 
(a) Government has always been aware of the antecedents of Osama bin Laden 
and the Taliban as also of its strong ties that Taliban continued to have with 
Pakistan, including with its military forces. 
(b) The Taliban. Osama bin Laden and the Al Qaeda network had turned 
Afghanistan into a centre of terrorism,  extremism and drug trafficking. Even 
before the terrorist attacks in the United States on 11th September, the United 
Nations Security Council had adopted resolutions, calling on the Taliban to 
hand over Osama Bin Laden, stop harbouring terrorist groups and close down 
all terrorist training camps. 
(c) Government has consistently advocated that terrorism is a global 
problem that requires a comprehensive international response targeted against 
terrorism and its sponsors everywhere in the world. It is also well established 
that the Taliban and the Al Qaeda network have links with terrorism in Jammu & 
Kashmir. Government's support to the ongoing military campaign against the 
Taliban and Al Qaeda network in Afghani stan is. therefore, in keeping with 
India's national interest. 
(d) Government has played a strong role in raising international awareness 
about the menace of terrorism and in strengthening global cooperation, including 
in the United Nations, in combating it. Government has also been actively engaged 
in international consultations on the post-Taliban political settlement and 
economic reconstruction of Afghanistan, including in the recently concluded 
meeting of Afghan factions held in Bonn. Germany, that led to an agreement on 
an interim Administration in Afghanistan.

Permanent seat in Security Council 
2667. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH : Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that France a nd Armenia have for the first time 
strongly come out with open and firm suport for a permanent seat for India in the 
United Nations Security Council (UNSC); 
(b) if so, the latest prospects for India to get a seat in the council; and 
(c) whether any piecemeal expansion of the Council has also been rejected 
by these two countries? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASW ANT SINGH): 
(a) During the debate in the UN General Assembly on reform and restructuring 
of the UN Security Council, France and Armenia made statements supporting 
the candidature of India for permanent membership in an expanded Security 
Council. On October 31,2001, the Permanent Representaive of France stated : 
"France envisaged the expansion of the UN Security Cuncil to include two 
developed industrialised countries and three developing countries from Asia, 
Africa and Latin America and Caribbean. France considered that Germay, Japan 
and India should occupy a permanent seat in the UN Security Council". On 31st 
October, 2001 the Armenian representative stated: "The issue of global geographic 
representation is of particular importance for us. We support the proposals to 
increase the regional representation, especially for the regions which are currently 
under represented such as Asia, Africa, Latin America and Caribbean. In this 
regard we believe that India deserves to be seriously considered as a candidate 
for permanent membership." Subsequently, while addressing the UN General 
Assembly on November 14,2001. the Foreign Minister of Armenia, Mr. Vartan 
Oskanian, reaffirmed Armenia's support for India's candidature for permanent 
membership of the UN Security Council. 
(b) There is growing support for India's candidature for permanent 
membership of the UN Security Council. The issue of the reform and the 
restructuring of the UN Security Council has been under discussion at the 
United Nations, for several years. The UN Charter stipulates that any change in 
the existing structure must be approved by two-thirds of the General Assembly 
including all Permanent Members of the Security Council. However, there is no 
consensus so far on some issues involved such as size of the expanded Council, 
the criteria for selection of new Permanent Members, the question of veto etc. 
(c) Yes, Sir. They do not favour piecemeal expansion of the Council.

26%. SHRIMATIVANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the details of the steps being taken by Govemir. nt for improvement in 
conditions of workers facing adverse working situations; and 
(b) the details of the steps being taken for elimination of evils of child labour 
and bonded labour? 
THEMIN1STEROFSTATEINTHEMINISTRYOFLABOUR (SHRIMUNI L 
ALL).: (a) and (b) The Government have formulated various schemes under existing 
Welfare Funds viz. (i) Beedi Workers Welfare Fund; (ii) Cine Workers Welfare Fund; 
(iii) Iron Ore Mines, Manganese Ore Mines and Chrome Ore Mines Welfare Fund; (iv) 
Lime Stone and Dolomite Mines Labour Welfare Fund; and (v) Mica Mines Labour 
Welfare Fund to provide social security and welfare measures like group insurance, 
medical care, education and housing facilities for the workers in these sectors. Recently, a 
social security scheme namely "Krishi 
140

Shramik Samajik Suraksha Yojana 2001" has been launched in 50 selected districts 
of the country. 
Various existing labour laws like the Workmen's Compensation Act, 
1923, The Minimum Wages Act, 1948, The Payment of Wages Act, 1936, The 
Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, The 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, The 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, The Bonded Labour 
System (Abolition) Act, 1976, Inter-State Migrant Workmen (RE & CS) Act, 
1979. The Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment 
and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996, and Building and Other Construction 
Workers' Welfare Cess Act, 1996 are applicable to the workers in unorganized 
sector. These Acts look after the interests of the workers in terms of wages, 
working hours, social security etc. 
The Central Government has enact ed the Bonded Labour System 
(Abolition) Act, 1976, which provides for identification, release and rehabilitation 
of bonded labours. The Act provides for setting up of Vigilance Committees at 
district and Sub-Divisional levels to monitor and review the incidence of bonded 
labour on a regular basis. In-order to assist the State Government in their task of 
rehabilitation of released bonded labourers, the Central Government has 
formulated a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for rehabilitation of bonded labour 
under which assistance up to the ceiling limit of Rs. 20,000 is given to each 
released bonded labourer. 
Under the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 
employment of children below the age of 14 is prohibited in 13 Occupations and 
57 Processes. Employers employing children in occupations and processes 
prohibited under the Act are liable to be prosecuted. The Government of India 
has also been implementing two schemes, for rehabilitation of children withdrawn 
from work, namely the scheme of National Child Labour Projects (NCLP) and the 
scheme of Grant-in-aid to Voluntary Organisations. The major activity under the 
NCLP is running special schools/centres for rehabilitation of children withdrawn 
from work tlirough non-formal education, vocational training, nutrition, health 
care, stipend etc. So far, 100NCLPshavebeensanctionedforcoverageof2.11 lakh 
children tlirough 3962 centres in 13 child labour endemic states.

services anchored on a norm of per capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in 
rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas.

and State level from the large sample surveys on consumer expenditure conducted by the 
National Sample Survey Organization (NSSO). The latest estimates of the number of 
poor persons are available for the year 1999-2000 based on the National Sample 
Survey data on consumer expenditure of the 55th Round. These are given in the 
statement (See below). The Planning Commission does not make estimates of the 
number of the very poor persons.

these projects? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATIVASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (e) The Approach paper to the Tenth Plan has identified Agriculture 
development as a core element of the Plan since growth in this sector is likely to 
165 

RAJ YA S ABHA [ 13 December, 2001 ] 
lead to the widest spread of benefits, especially to the rural poor including 
agricultural labour. Infrastructure development, where gaps are large and private 
sector cannot be expected to step in significantly, the role of government may 
have to be restructured. It will have to increase in some areas of infrastructure 
development which are unlikely to attr act private investment e.g. rural 
infrastructure and road development. In others e.g. 'telecommunications, power, 
ports, etc., the private sector can play a much larger role provided an appropriate 
policy framework is in place. Here, the role of the Government needs to change 
to facilitate such investment as much as possible while still remaining a public 
sector service provider for quite some time. In all these areas, the role of 
government in creating and maintaining a modern regulatory system for ensuring 
a fair deal for consumers, transparency and accountability, and a level playing 
field is also extremely important. Redefining the role of the Government to reflect 
the changed circumstances facing the economy must be an important aspect of 
future strategy. 
This redefinition is necessary both at the Central Government level and 
also at State Government level.' 
The Planning Commission is in the process of formulation of Tenth Five 
Year Plan (2002-2007). Public programmes giving boost to agriculture and 
infrastructure activities in the country over the next five years will be included in 
the Tenth Five Year Plan.

Standing Committee of Secretaries to assist the CCEA and CCER have also been

REFERENCE TO THE TERRORISTS ATTACK ON THE 
PARLIAMENT HOUSE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I rise to make reference to the 
cowardly and dastardly act of the terr orists, who attacked the Parliament 
Building yesterday, the 13 th December, 2001. It has shocked not only the 
entire Nation but also the conscience of freedom - loving humankind all over 
the world.   No words are strong  enough  to  condemn  this heinous act. 
As we are aware, seven persons, including four from my security, 
namely Shri Jagdish Prasad Yadav, Security Assistant, Watch and Ward, 
Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Shrimati Kamlesh Kumari of C.R.P.F., Shri 
Ghanshyam, Shri Nanak Chand, Shri  Ram Pal, Shri Om Prakash, all 
belonging to Delhi Police, Shri Desh Raj, Gardner belonging to CPWD were 
killed. Watch and Ward staff were unarmed, but showed great presence of 
mind. At least thirty persons, including  some security personnel were injured 
in the terrorists shoot-out and* some of them are in a critical condition. Our 
sympathies go to the victims of the attack and the bereaved families. 
Our security personnel and Watch an d Ward staff deserve praise for 
their alertness and devotion to their duty in highest traditions in intercepting 
and shooting down the terrorists. Their timely action averted a major 
catastrophe. 
I hope the whole House joins me in condemning this brutal and 
barbaric attack. We resolve to fight unitedly terrorism with grit and 
determination and shall eliminate it. This House extends its heartfelt 
condolences to the affected families in their hour of grief. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the memory of those who laid down their precious lives in 
this tragedy. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.)

OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Honourable Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Arangil Sreedharan, a former Member of this House, on the 
13th December, 2001, at the age of 78. 
Born at Badagara, Kerala, in March, 1923, Shri Sreedharan had his education at 
Badagara, Mangalore, Calicut and Vellore. A dedicated political and social worker, 
Shri Sreedharan'took an active part in the "Quit India Movement" in 1942. He was 
also associated with various trade unions and championed the cause of the weaker 
sections of the society. He was imprisoned on several occasions in connection 
with the agitation of farmers and workers. Shri Sreedharan was the Chairman 
of the Indian Socialist Party from 1961 to 1971. 
Shri Sreedharan started his legislative career as a Member of the Fourth Lok 
Sabha. He represented the State of Kerala in this House from July, 1988 to July, 
1994. He also served as the Minister of State of Commerce from April, 1990 to 
November, 1990. 
In the passing away of Shri Sreedharan the country has lost a freedom 
fighter, an active social worker and a veteran parliamentarian. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Arangil Sreedharan. 
I also wish to place on record the sacr ifice of Shri Matbar Singh, Security 
Assistant of Watch and Ward Service, Rajya Sabha Secretariat, who was 
injured in the terrorists' attack on Parliament on the 13th December, 2001 and 
succumbed to his injuries on the 16th December, 2001. 
Shri Matbar Singh showed an exemplary courage and devotion to duty by 
closing the building Gate No. 11, even though hit by bullets 
1 

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2001] 
in the terrorists' shoot-out thereby averting an unimaginable disaster. His 
selfless and courageous deed has thus set an example for others to emulate 
and all of us feel proud. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Matbar Singh. 
I request Members to rise in their pl aces and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General w ill convey to the members of the 
bereaved families our sense of profound sorrow and deep sympathy.

Toning up of corporate governance 
2915. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any step to tone up Corporate 
Governance; 
(b) whether inview of the market manipulations in recent past it has 
become imperative to bring about n ecessary changes for reforming the 
systems of Corporate Governance; and 
(c) what steps Government contemplates to take in near future in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SING H): (a) to (c) Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (SEBI) set up a Committee on Corporate 
Governance on May 7, 1999 to promote and raise the standards of Corporate 
Governance. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, SEBI 
directed stock exchanges to amend their 
56 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
listing agreements to implement the mandatory recommendations of the 
Committee. SEBI has made some of the best practices of corporate 
governance mandatory, through a phased programme. The board of directors 
of a company shall have an optimum  combination of executive and nog-
executive directors with not less than 50% of the boards consisting of non-
executive directors. A qualified and independent audit committee is required 
to be set up, which will meet at least thrice a year. The annual reports of 
companies are required to have a separate section on corporate governance. 
The new clause in the listing agreement also lays down board procedures 
including the frequency of board meetings. Further, a director shall not be a 
member in more than 10 committees or act as Chairman of more than five 
committees across all companies in which he is a Director. Shareholders are 
to be provided information in case of appointment of a new Director or re-
appointment of a Director. A board committee is to be formed to look into 
redressal of shareholder and investor complaints. The Government has also 
instituted a National Award for Excellence in Corporate Governance.

workers of sick and loss making PSUs, particularly those where wage 
revision has not been effected after 1.1.1987 or 1.1.1992, as the case may be,

respectively. The compensation of retr enched employees is governed under 
the Industrial Dispute Act, further liberalization of whose provisions are 
being examined by the Ministry of Labour. 
Further, in pursuance of the Industrial Policy of the Government, to 
provide a safety net to the employees of the organized sector, a National 
Renewal Fund (NRF) was set up by the Government in February, 1992. 
Government has been providing fund from NRF, for meeting expenses 
towards voluntary retirement of employees of CPSUs as also for 
rehabilitation of the employees of the organized

sector consisting of CPSUs.  Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion 
adminsterd the scheme till 31.3.2001.

scheme for Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment of rationalised employees 
of Central PSUs with an objective to reorient the rationalised employees of 
CPSUs through short duration training programmes to encourage them to avail of 
opportunities of self employment after their separation from the PSEs due to VRS 
or retrenchement due to closure of the enterprise. In order to have wide coverage of

† 2935. SHRI KHAN GHUFRAN ZAHIDI: Will the Minister of FINANCE

77

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Yes sir. The news item refers to the 
observations made by the Finance Ministers at the Development Committee 
Meeting of the Boards of Governors of the World Bank and the International 
Monetary Fund held in Ottawa on November 18, 2001 under the 
chairmanship of the Finance Minister of India (Shri Yashwant Sinha). The 
Ministers reviewed the impact of the September 11, terrorist attacks and their 
aftermath on developing countries. They recognized that poverty in many 
developing countries was likely to worsen as these events have deepened the 
pre-existing global economic slowdown, which had already led to weaker 
exports and commodity prices, and have other more specific impacts; e.g., 
increased refugee movements within co untries and across borders; reduced 
private investment flows due to increased risk aversion in financial markets; 
reduced tourism revenues; and increased trade transaction costs. 
(b) and (c) The longer term economic impact of the terrorist attack in USA 
and the subsequent war in Afghanistan on the Indian economy will depend 
upon the duration and intensity of the war and its impact on global demand 
and trade. There has been some effect  of the war on Indian exports, stock 
markets, tourism, heightened risk aversion of foreign investors and the 
foreign exchange market. However, Indi a's share in international trade and 
finance is marginal and the Government has adopted credible economic 
reforms with a focus on generation of employment and reduction of poverty. 
Mereover, in its mid-term review of the monetary and credit policy for the 
year 2001-02, announced in October 2001, the Reserve Bank of India has 
projected 5-6 per cent growth for the Indian economy for the year 2001-2002.

BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Under the Kisan Credit card (KCC) Scheme, 
the farmers avail crop loans to meet th eir production and contingency needs. 
Under National Agricultural insurance Scheme (NAIS), the fanners availing loans 
through Kisan Credit Cards for raising notified crops, within the purview of the 
provisions of the Scheme, are covered for crop losses only. The Scheme of

notified crop for widespread calamities and on an 'individual basis' in limited areas 
for localised calamities, such as, hailstorm, landslide, cyclone and floods, on an 
experimental basis. The defined area (i.e. unit of insurance) may be Gram 
panchayat, Mandal, Hobli, Circle, Phirka, Block, Taluka, etc., as decided by the 
State Government/Union Territory but  each participating State/ Union 
Territory is requird to leach the level of Gram Panchayat within a period of 3

RBI's Suggestion on NPAs 
2972. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
» 
(a) whether it is a fact that RBI expre ssed its concern over the potential 
danger of addition to the stock of new Non-Performing Assets; 
(b) if so, what are the suggestions made by RBI; and 
(c) what are Government's comments thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
reported that as the regulator of the banking system in the country, it is 
concerned about the additions to the stock of non-performing assets (NPAs) 
of the banks. 
(b) and (c) Government and RBI have been emphasizing the need for 
proper credit appraisal an d the exercise of due cau tion to prevenj adverse 
selection of borrowers. Banks have been advised to formulate comprehensive 
loan policy including appraisal standards/procedures, exposure limits, 
documentation standards, sectoral exposure limits, delegation of powers 
review procedure etc. Banks have also been advised to strengthen their risk 
management system by putting in  place institutional framework for 
identifying, monitoring and manageme nt of risk. RBI has put in place a 
system of circulating amongst the banks and financial institutions, the names 
of defaulting borrowers of Rs. One crore and above (including suit filed 
accounts) and those of wilful defaulters  of Rs. 25 lakhs and above, which 
can be used by them while considering the requests for credit limits by such 
borrowers. Credit Information Bureau ha s also been set up to disseminate 
information on borrowers to the banks.

BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
issued revised guidelines in January, 2001 on entry of new banks in the private 
sector. These guidelines, inter-alia, stipulate initial minimum paid-up capital for a 
new bank shall be Rs. 200 crore (which shall be increased to Rs. 300 crore in

maintaining arms-length relationship with business entities in the promoter 
group, no large industrial house shall promote a new bank, maintenance of 
minimum capital adequacy ratio of 10%, permitting conversion of NBFCs with 
good trek record into banks etc. RBI has reported that it has received 10 
applications which were referred to a High-Level Advisory Committee set up by 
RBI and it has submitted its recommendations, which are under examination of 
RBI.

Decline in production capacity of Mumbai High 
3005. SHRI NANA DE SHMUKH: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Mumbai High which commenced production of 
oil in 1976 did produce 4 lakh barrels of oil per day between 1985 and 1989; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the production has declined to 2.2 lakh 
barrels and the production of gas has also come down; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to boost the production of both these items 
again? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) to (c) The 
Mumbai High field of Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. (ONGC) started 
production in 1976 and entered in the declining phase of production from 1990-91, 
which is a natural phenomenon for any aging field, thus, while the Mumbai 
High field reached its peak production of 4 lakh barrels of oil per day during the 
period 1985-89, the average production has declined gradually to about 2.20 lakh 
barrels per day of oil in November 2001. The gas production has also come down 
to 14.17 million standard cubic metres per day (MMSCMD) in November 2001 
from the peak level of 26.83 MMSCMD. 
(d) In order to improve the recovery of oil and gas from the Mumbai High 
(M.H.) field, ONGC has taken up the redevelopment of M.H. North and M.H. 
South Fields, which envisages an incremental production of about 75 million 
metric tonnes of oil and oil equivalent of gas over a 30 years time-frame.

Delhi as Tourist Friendly City 
3019. SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA: Will the Minister of TOURISM AND 
CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that tourists visit only in a holistic perspective; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that we are lagging behind in inflow of tourists and 
even smaller countries arc much ahead of us; 
(c) if so, what arc the figures of tourist inflow during the last three years; and 
(d) what steps arc being taken to make Delhi a tourist-fricndly-city especially 
for foreigners? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI JAGMOHAN): 
(a) Yes; by and large. 
(b) During the year 2000, India received less number of tourists as compared to 
the countries like Japan, Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia. 
(c) 2.36 million, 2.48 million and 2.64 million foreign tourists visited 
India in 1998, 1999 and 2000 respectively. 
(d) Various steps taken by the Government to make Delhi a tourist friendly 
city include installation of signages at important monuments, installation of 
Touch Screen Kiosks to get ready access to information at various tourist places 
and installation of tourist guidance system "HARK" at Red Fort. A project on 
"Remote Presence" to enable a tourist to have a complete video view as seen 
from the top of the Qutub Minar has also been completed Festivals 
 
160 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
such as Shalimar festival, Qutub Festival and Garden Festival are also organised 
regularly. 
Dissemination of Indian Culture Abroad 
3020. PROF. M. S ANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of 
TOURISM AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken, so far, by Government to disseminate the traditional and 
ancient art and culture of the country outside India; and 
(b) the details of the NRIs who have come forward to enter into the venture 
of dissemination of culture abroad? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) 
The Department of Culture has been pursuing an active policy of bilateral cultural 
cooperation with other countries with the objective of renewing and 
strengthening cultural links and with a view to project India's Culture abroad. 
However, one of the objectives of the Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR) 
under Ministry of External Affairs' is to promote greater awareness of India's 
cultural heritage abroad. Towards this end, the Council has set up and maintains 
14 cultural centres which are functioning under the overall policy guidelines of the 
Indian Missions in the respective countries. 
(b) There are a number of NRIs an d Indian Associations abroad who 
undertake dissemination of Indian culture at their own initiative, not necessarily 
involving our Missions abroad. Such details are not available with the 
Government.

Summary of the Provisions of Lease cum Management Agreement, Hotel

—Agreement between (1) Kumarakruppa Frontier Hotels Private Limited 
(Lessor/Licensor, new company in which the business undertaking and assets 
and liabilities of Ashok Hotel vests after the demerger); (2) Bidder 
(Lessee/Licensee) 
• Lease: ITDC's ownership of the land and building in which Ashok Hotel 
is situated transferred to Kumarakruppa Frontier Hotels Private Limited 
through demerger. The premises to be further leased to the Bidder. 
• Licensor Assets: Fixed assets, other than premises, of Ashok Hotel, to be 
handed over to the Bidder. These asse ts to revert to the Licensor on 
expire of the Agreement. 
• Term: The term of the sub-lease is 30 years, renewable by mutual 
consent for another period of 30 years. There is a sub lease granted for the 
Airport Restaurant, Bangalore valid till 2005. 
• Consideration: The annual consideration to be the higher of a Minimum 
Guaranteed Annual Payment or an amount equivalent to 16.5% of Gross 
Turnover. 
• Upfront Payment: The Bidder to pay the discounted value of 50% of the 
annual payments to be paid over 30 years. The

50% of the consideration to be paid annually.

adequate job opportunities to the members of the Scheduled 
Castes / Scheduled Tribes, Physically Handicapped persons and 
other socially disadvantaged sections. In the event of any 
reduction in the strength of the employees, the physically 
handicapped persons are retrenched at the end. 
The Bidder to offer employment to all the Employees on the terms and 
conditions that are not inferior to those applicable on the closing date 
including the voluntary retirement scheme as per the guidelines of the 
Department of Public Enterprises. The Bidder not to retrench any of it's the 
Employees for a period of one year from the Closing Date other than any 
dismissal or termination of Employees as per staff regulations or applicable 
law. 
The Lessor/Licensor has fulfilled all obligations in respect of the Employees. 
• Outstanding Government Dues: The bidder to directly pay by a banker's cheque 
all outstanding demands towards property taxes, compounding charges, and 
other municipal and Government dues. 
• Transfer of Business: Current assets loss current liabilities, employees, 
contracts, goodwill and contigent liabilities of Hotel Ashok to be transferred 
to the Bidder for a consideration equivalent to the next current assets as 
on March 31, 2001. 
• Post Closing Adjustment: Any reduction in the net current assets amount from 
March 31, 2001 to the closing date to be paid to the bidder and vice 
versa. 
• Security Deposit: An amount equal to two year's annual payment to be paid to 
the Lessor as security deposit fee of interest and to be refunded at the end of 
the term. The deposit amount to be increased proportionately with increase 
in the annual payment.

and appearing in the balance sheet of the unit, list of employees, litigation and

(Ms. BUOY A CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Availability of water in the 
country varies both temporally as well as spatially. As a result, a number of areas 
receive excessive rainfall and get flooded while other areas face drought like 
situation due to scarcity of the rainfall. Rashtriya barh Ayog (1988) assessed 
that about 34 million hectares of area in the country is prone to floods. The 
state wise details are given in the Statement I (See below).

to areas in Rajasthan, Kutch and Saur ashtra region, have per capita water 
availability below 1000 cubic metre per year, which according to certain International 
organizations represents a scarcity condition. The names of basins covering 
different states and the per capita water availability therein is given in the 
Statement II (see below) 
(c) and (d) Requirement of water is closely related to population, demand for 
food, production of ind jstrial items, production of energy and preserving ecology. 
The availability of water for use for diverse purposes has increased over the Plan 
periods by creation of the live storage capacity of 177 (BCM) by construction of 
large dams upto 1995. An additional live storage capacity of 75 BCM will be 
created on completion of dams, which are under various statges of 
construction. Proposals to take up additional dams to create a live storage   
capacity   of   132   BCM   are    also   under   formulation/

* 369. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKA RASU : Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in a book on  ancient India prescribed for Xlth

(b) if so, the paragraphs deleted by CBSE; and

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR.

(c) Contents of the said^aragraph is considered objectionable and likely to

Statement 
The Varna System 
Religion influenced the formation of so cial classes in India in a peculiar 
way. In other ancient societies the dutie s and functions of social classes were 
fixed by law which was largely enforced by the state. But in India Varna laws 
enjoyed the sanction of both the state and   religion.   The   functions  of  
priests,  warriors,   peasants  and 
200 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
labourers were defined in law and supposed to have been laid down by divine 
agencies. Those who departed from their functions and were found guilty of 
offences were subjected to secular punishments. They had also to perform rituals 
and penances, all differing according to the Varna. Each Varna was given not 
only a social but also a ritualistic recognition. In course of time Varnas or social 
classes and jatis or castes were made hereditary by law and religion. All this was 
done to ensure that vaishyas produce and pay taxes and shudras serve as labourers 
so that brahmanas act as priests and kshatriyas as rulers. Based on the division of 
labour and specialization of occupations, the peculiar institution of the caste system 
certainly helped the growth of society and economy at the initial stage. The 
Varna system contributed to the development of the state. The producing and 
labouring classes were disarmed, and gradually each caste was pitted against the 
other in such a manner that the oppressed ones could not combine against the 
privileged classes. 
The need of carrying out their respective functions was so strongly ingrained in 
the minds of the various classes that ordinarily they would never think of 
deviating from their dharma. The Bhagavadgita taught that people should lay down 
their lives in defence of their own dharma rather than adopt the dharma of others, 
which would prove dangerous. The lower orders worked hard in the firm belief that 
they would deserve a better life in the next world or birth. This belief lessened 
the intensity and frequency of tensions and conflicts between those who actually 
produced and those who lived off these producers as princes, priests, officials, 
soldiers and big merchants. Hence the necessity for exercising coercion against the 
lower orders was not so strong in "Ancient India". What was done by slaves and 
other producing sections in Greece and Rome under the threat of whip was done by 
the vaishyas and shudra as out of conviction formed through brahmanical 
indoctrinations and the Varna system.

Statement I 
Macro Management of Agriculture 'Supplementation/Complementation of 
States' Efforts through Work Plan' 
Objective: Macro Management scheme will  aim  at  all  round 
development   in   agriculture   through   Work   Plans 
prepared by State. These include. 
• Reflection   of  local   needs/crop/regions  specific/ 
priorities etc. 
• Providing flexibility and autonomy to States; 
• Optimum utilization of scarce financial resource; 
• Maximisation of returns; 
• Removal of regional imbalances. 
Salient features: It has been decided to move away from schematic approach 
to Macro management mode by integrating 27 Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes (a list is annexed). The previous 
pattern of rigid uniformly structured Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes, permitting little or no flexibility, which resulted in 
large unutilised balances with states has been dispensed 
with. Integration of Centrally Sponsored Schemes under 
Macro management approach will enhance the productivity 
of support programmes and accord greater flexibility to 
State Governments to develop and pursue activities on the 
basis of regional priorities.  It is, 
230 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
thus, a major step towards ach ieving decentralization in 
pursuance of restoring primacy  of States in agricultural 
development planning. The Central Government will 
supplement/complement the State Government's efforts 
through regionally differentiated Work Plans comprising 
crop/area/ target group specific interventions, formulated in 
an interactive mode and implemented in spirit of 
partnership with the States. 
Pattern of The outlay of the Work Plan would be shared by 
assistance: the Centre and the States in the ratio of 90:10. In the 
case of North-Eastern States, however, the entire 
expenditure will be borne by the Government of India. 
Central assistance for Work Plans will be in the ratio of 80 
by grants and 20% by loans.

Central Schemes for Medicinal and Aromatic Plants etc.  
2747.   SHRIMATI   CHANDRA   KALA   PANDEY:   Will   the 
Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the salient features of the Centrally sponsored schemes of 
Development of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants; Development of Roots and 
Tuber Crops; Development of Mushroom, Bee keeping; Scheme for 
foundation and certified seed production of vegetable crops, State Land Use 
Boards; Oilseeds production programme; 
(b) the criteria for allocating funds u nder each scheme to States and 
corresponding central share; whether these funds would be given to States as 
100 per cent grant or whether it would follow the usual 70-30 (loan/grant) 
formula for Plan assistance; and 
(c) the State-wise details of proposals received, funds released and utilized 
during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE  
(SHRI  HUKUMDEO  NARAYAN  YADAV): 
(a) These schemes aim to increase the production and productivity of the 
respective crops through Supply of quality planting material of improved 
varieties and making available technical know-how to growers through 
trainings and demonstrations. The scheme on State 
236

Land Use Board envisages implementation of 19 point recommendations of 
the National Land Use Policy and promote scientific land useteview of land 
based programmes at State level etc. The scheme on Bee-keeping aims at increasing 
productivity of crops through enhanced pollination. 
These Schemes, except the scheme on Oilseeds Production Programme, 
have now been subsumed, since October, 2000, in the scheme on macro 
management of agriculture-Supplementation/ complementation of States' efforts 
through work plans. Under these schemes States have greater flexibility to prioritise 
their needs. The programmes of these schemes can now be pursued by the StatcsUTs 
through their work plans. 
(b) The approved pattern of assistance under the scheme is in the 
ratio of 90:10 for the Centre and the States respectively except in the 
case of North-Eastern States including Sikkim who are being given 
100% Central assistance. The Central assistance released to the States . 
would be in the ratio of 80% grant and 20% loan. The allocation of 
funds under the scheme is made to States-UTs after mutual discussion 
with them on their work plans. However, States can make further 
allocations on individual interventions according to their 
developmental priorities based on work plans. 
Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme on Oilseeds Production Programme the 
criteria for allocation of funds is done on the basis of area as well as the 
procduction of Oilseeds Crops in a particular State. 
(c) In order to avail assistance under macro management scheme, 
each StatcAJT submits its proposals in form of work plans which are 
discussed between the Department of Agriculture & Cooperation and 
the StatesUTs concerned for a llocation of funds. Statements

Ban on fishing in Arabian Sea 
2748. SHRI  A.  VIJAYA RAG HAVAN:  Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to stop fishing of certain fish 
varieties like shark, in the Arabian Sea; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government would consider to ban fishing of certain varieties 
of fish from our sea; and 
247 

RAJYA SABHA      [18 December, 2001] 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) Government of India, 
Ministry of Environment and Forests (MOEF) had issued a notification in July, 
2001 imposing ban on hunting of sharks and rays considering the fact that they have 
become rare and endangered due to over-exploitation to meet the increased 
international demand for their fins, meat, etc. This decision is reported to 
have been taken based on a scientific publication of Central Marine Fisheries 
Research Institute (CMFRI), Cochin. 
A large number of representations from various quarters were received 
asserting that the aforesaid ban would adversely affect the livelihood opportunities of 
large number of fishermen. A meeting was convened by MOEF recently to discuss 
the issue with the experts and scientists of various institutes in the country. Based 
on the views expressed in this meeting it was decided to give a three years research 
project on the issue to CMFRI and Zoological Survey of India to assess 
population status of individual species and quantum harvested annually. In the 
interim period the MOEF have decided to restrict the ban to ten shark species that 
are considered critically endangered and vulnerable by the International Union 
for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

† 2752. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
SHRI RAJIV RAN J AN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there ha s been a constant decrease in the 
cultivated land holding of farmers in the country during the last many years; 
(b) if so, the average size of the cultivat ed land-holding in the country at 
present; 
(c) whether it is a fact that cultivation in this size of a holding has become 
economically unviable; and 
(d) if so, Government reaction in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. As per 
Agricultural Censuses 1970-71, 1976-77, 1980-81, 1985-86 and 1990-91, 
the average size per holding (in hectare) was 2.28, 2.00, 1.84, 1.69 and 1.55 
respectively. The latest all-India results of Agricultural Census relate to 
agricultural year 1990-91. 
(c) and (d) The viability of an agricultural holding depands upon a variety 
of factors including agro-climatic, level of use of agricultural input, 
availability of irrigation facilities, crop variety sown and the entrepreneurial 
skill of the farmer. No conclusive evidence is available regarding 
relationship between size of the holding and its economic viability.

Shortfall in Sugarcane Production 
2759. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that sugarcane production in the current seasons is 
likely to be 280 mts. against a target of 300 mil. tonnes last year and 
Government's target 325 mil. tonnes; and 
(b) if so, what are the reasons for this shortfall and the steps being taken to 
ensure higher production next year? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) According to the first 
Advance Estimates for 2001-02, the production of sugarcane in the country 
during 2001-02 is likely to be 280.0 million tonnes against the estimated 
production of 300.3 million tonnes in 2000-01 and a production target of 325.0 
million tonnes for 2001-02. The Advance estimates are subject to revision. 
(b) The fall in sugarcane production during 2001-02 is expected to 
265 

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2001] 
be due to moisture stress during monsoon season in the States of Andhra 
Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra. However, good rainfall in southern 
States like Andhra Pradesh, Karnatak a and Tamil Nadu during the post-
monsoon season has improved the prospects of the crop. The production of 
sugarcane shows a long-term upward trend, albeit with minor fluctuations. 
Further, research by Indian Council of Agriculture Research has enabled 
development of new varieties like Co 85004, Co 87025, Co 86032, Co 
87044, Co 91010, Co 8371, Co 86249, Pant 90223, CoS 91230, Co 87263 and 
Co 8268. The cultivation of newly developed sugarcane varieties alongwith 
improved package of practices will be helpful in improving sugarcane 
production in the country. 
Pesticide Scarcity in A.P. 
2760. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister 
of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:- 
(a) whether it is a fact that cotton gr owers in Andhra Pradesh are facing 
pesticide scarcity due to imposition of ban on American Cargo carriers that 
bring pesticides; 
(b) the quantity of such pesticides needed for cotton growers in that State 
and how much quantity has been met, till date; and 
(c) the steps being taken by the Central Government to arrange 
immediate import of pesticides and to keep stocks to meet such requirement? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY. OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) There is no pesticides 
scarcity in Andhra Pradesh for the cotton growers. However, the Government 
of Andhra Pradesh has informed th at because of uncertainty and non-
availability of commercial flights in the United States due to post September 
11 attacks, there is delay in the supply  of "Avaunt" manufactured by M/s. 
E.I. Dupont India Ltd. and and "Tracer" manufactured by M/s. Denocil 
Limited in Andhra Pradesh State. Bu t a large number of indigenously 
manufactured insecticides which can be  used as substitutes to these two 
pesticides are available in plenty in the market.

† 2773. SHRI JANESHWAR MISH RA: Will the Minister of

(a) whether it is a fact that the country is forced to import huge quantities 
of fertilizers and pesticides/Insectic ides; in view of the increasing 
competition and crops in the agricultural sector, and diminishing land-
fertility; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that pesticides/in secticides are till now being used 
which are quite fatal for environment and the birds; and

action-plan, the farmers would have to depend mostly on foreign 
manures and pesticides/insecticides in future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) 
In the case of fertilizers, the country has now achieved a high degree of self-
sufficiency in Nitrogenous and Phosphatic fertilizers; however, there is a total 
dependence on import for Potassic fertili zers because of the absence of its 
commercial exploitable reserves in the country. During 2000-01, out of total 
consumption of 355.6 LMTs of all the chemical fertilizers (in product terms), 
only about 34 LMTs of fertilizers were imported, which is less than 10%. On 
the other hand, India is a net exporter of pesticides. Its exports have shown an 
impressive growth over the last 5 years and totalled Rs. 1083 crores in 2000-
01 (April-February) as against the import of Rs. 194 crores during this 
period. Thus, the indigenous capacity of pesticides is adequate to meet the 
requirement of domestic demand. 
(c) All bird species are affected by pesticides/insecticides. However, the 
species found in and around farmlands are affected more. Some instances 
have also been noticed regarding decline in soil health and productivity due to 
inadequate and imbalanced use of chemical fertilizers in certain parts of the 
country.
