Olive Ridley Turtles 
2781. SHRI     ANANTA     SETHI:     Will     the     Minister     of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large num ber of Olive Ridley Turtles, coming 
every year to lay their eggs in the river bed and mouths 
294 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
Rushikulya and Devi rivers near Gahirmatha Wild Life Sanctuary in Orissa 
are killed by poachers; 
(b) whether it is a fact that a large num ber of sea turtles are now coming 
in groups, as every year; and 
(c) if so, the details of steps taken to save these rare species from 
poachers? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) It is a fact that  large number of Olive Ridley Turtles 
come every year for mass nesting on Orissa Coast particularly in Gahirmatha 
Wildlife Sanctuary, Rushikulya river mouth and Devi river mouth. Chief 
Wildlife Warden, Orissa has reported that Olive Ridley Turtle has been 
killed by poachers. However, mortalit ies on account of Olive Ridley Turtles 
being caught in fishing nets are reported from time to time. Steps have been 
taken to check such mortalities include:- 
1. Mechanised fishing has been banned in the marine waters within 5 
kms. from the coast line in Orissa. 
2. Use of Turtle Exclusive Device (TED ) in mechanised fishing trawlers 
has been made mandatory and the fishermen are being trained for using the 
same. 
3. Officers from Forest Department, Department of Fisheries and Coast 
Guards regularly patrol the area to check illegal fishing. 
4. Protection camps with communicati on facilities (wireless network) 
have been set up at strategic points for - effective communication in the area. 
5. Public awareness campaigns are organised through media Non-
Government Organisations. 
6. Better coordination is maintained at district level in the coastal districts 
for providing effective protection to Olive Ridley Turtles.

Centrally sponsored educational schemes 
2810. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the salient features of the centrally sponsored schemes 
of Joint GOI-Un Programme for Primary Education; 
Sarvasiksha Abhiyan; National Programme for Women's 
Education; Literacy Campaign; Operation Restoration support 
to NGOs in the field of Adult Education (earlier Shramic 
Vidyapeeth); Counting Education for New Literates; Culture 
Exchange Programme; 
(b) what are the criteria fo r allocating funds under each 
scheme    to    States    and    the    corresponding    Central    share; 
320 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
whether these funds are given to States as 100 percent grant or the usual 
70/30 (loan/grant) formula is followed for Plan assistance; and 
(c) the details of proposals received, funds released and utilization for last 
three years. State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. (S HRIMATI) RITA VERM A): (a) 
The salient features of various centrally sponsored schemes referred to in the 
Question are as follows:— 
1. Janshala (Joint GOI-UN Programme): It is a community-based primary 
education programme with the objective of making primary education more 
accessible and effective, especially for girls and children of deprived 
communities, marginalised groups, SC/ST/ minorities, working children and 
children with special needs. The programme is a collaborative effort of the 
Government of India and five UN agencies viz. UNDP, UNICEF, UNESCO 
ILO and UNFPA to provide programme support to the ongoing efforts 
towards achieving Universalisation of Elementary Education. The programme 
presently covers 139 blocks and 10 cities in 31 districts spread over 9 States i.e. 
Andhra Pradesh, Chattis garh, Jharkhand, Karnat aka, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Orissa Rajasthan and U ttar Pradesh. The UN agencies have 
committed a contribution of US$ 20 million as a grant for this programme. 
2. Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA): It is a newly launched scheme with a 
holistic and integrated approach to acheive the objective of Universalisation of 
Elementary Education. The programme aims to provide useful and quality 
elementary education of 8 years to a ll children in the 6—14 age group by 
2010. The programme will cover all the districts in the country. The 
expenditure on the programme will be shared between Centre & States in the 
ratio 85:15 in the 9th Plan, 75:25 in the 10th Plan and 50:50 in the 11th Plan 
and in the subsequent Plan periods. 
321 

RAJYA SABHA       [18 December, 2001] 
3. National Programme for Women's Education: At present no such scheme is 
under operation. 
4. Literacy Campaigns and Operation Restoration: The Total Literacy 
Companies (TLC) is the principal strategy of the National Literacy Mission 
for eradication of illiteracy. Besides imparting functional literacy, it also 
include interventions for encreasing enrolement and retention of children in 
schools, immunisation, propagation of small family norms, promotion of 
maternity and child care, women's equally and empowerment, peace and 
communal harmony etc. On conclusion of TLC, Post Literacy Programme 
(PLP) is taken up for consolidation of lit eracy skills and integration of skill 
development programmes. Out of 598 districts in the country, 574 districts 
are covered under Adult Education programmes. The funding pattern is ratio 
of 2:1 and 4:1 between Centre and State Governments for normal and tribal 
districts respectively. 
5. Continuing Education: The scheme aims at providing further learning 
opportunities to neo-Literatcs by setting up Continuing Education Cetnres, to 
serve population of 2000-2500 by providing facilities of library, reading 
room, learning centre etc. The Central Government provides 100% funding 
for the first three years which is to be  shared between the Central and State 
Governments equally during the next two years. The scheme has been 
sanctioned to 112 districts in 18 States and Union Territories. Recurring 
assistance is provided to the Nodal and Continuing Education Centre @ Rs. 
45,000/- and 25,000/- per year respectively. A non-recurring assistance is also 
provided on the same scale once in five years. 
6. Jan Shikshan Sansthan (formerly known as Shramik Vidyapceth): The 
scheme aims to provide polyvalent or multi-faceted adult education 
programme by improving the vocational skills and quality of life of its 
beneficiaries, which are mostly nco-litcratcs, semi-literates and non-Literates. 
It concentrates on the socio-economically backward and educationally dis-
advantaged groups of urban/rural population, such as neo- litcrates, semi-
literates, SCs, STs, women and girls slum dwellers, migrant workers, etc. 
7. Culture Exchange Programme: Ministry of Culture is the nodal 
322 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
agency for formulation of Cultural Exchange Programmes and monitoring 
their implementation. Cultural Exchange Programmes incorporate specific 
provisions for exchanges such as visits of professors, experts, scholars, 
artists, writers, performing troupes sports teams, exhibitions, youth and 
children's groups, radio and TV programmes, awards of scholarships, training 
in specialised fields, institutional cooperation and participation in 
international, fairs, exhibitions, festivals etc. They also include items for 
establishment of institutional links, especially between universities and other 
institutions of higher education and re search. No State-wise releases have 
been made by this Department under these programmes. 
(b) and (c) The entire Central share for the above schemes is released as 
grant. Funds are released  to the concerned States/State Implementation 
Societies as per the funding pattern of various schemes, progress of 
expenditure, availability of unspent ba lances etc. In the case of Janshala 
(Joint GOI-UN Programme), funds we re released by the concerned UN 
agencies directly to the project States upto March, 2001 and therefore figures 
of expenditure are reported. In the case of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), 
since the programme was launched during the last financial year only, 
figures of utilisation of funds are yet to become available. In the case of 
schemes for Adult Education, unutilised funds during the year are allowed to 
be carried over to the next financial year. The information relating to funds 
sanctioned/expenditure on the above lines is given in the statement.

Outlay for Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
2815. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the objectives of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan; 
(b) how the States would be participating in the scheme; 
(c) how many institutions are planne d to be opened in the next five 
years, State-wise; 
(d) the funds outlay for this, State-wise; and 
(e) whether the system would go through the same syllabus, as presently 
adopted for elementary education? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMEN T (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) 
The objectives of SSA are as follows: 
All children in school/Education Guarantee Centre/Alternate School, 
'Back to School' camp by 2003; 
All children complete five years of primary schooling by 2007; 
330 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
All children complete eight years of schooling by 2010; 
Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life; 
Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 2007 
and at elementary education level by 2010; 
Unviersal retention by 2010. 
(b) The Central and state Governments will together implement the Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan in partnership with the local Governments and the 
community. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan envisages a long term partnership 
between the Centre and the State. The funds required for the plan would be 
shared between the Centre and states in the ratio of 85:15 for IXth plan, 75:25 
for the Xth Plan and 50:50 thereafter. The States would be preparing District 
Elementary Education Plans (DEEPs) and they would be responsible for 
implementation also. 
(c) Opening of new primary and upper primary schools would depend on 
local needs as reflected in the Dist rict Elementary Education Plans, 
according to the norms. 
(d) For the year 2001-2002, Rs. 500 crores have been provided at the All 
India level for this scheme. However, State level allocation would depend on 
the demand projected as per norms in the District Elementary Education Plan. 
(e) The syllabus in schools will be the prerogative of the State 
Government. Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan encourages decentralization of the 
process of curriculum development so th at local context specific issues are 
highlighted. It also encourages attempts to reduce the load of non-
comprehension by facilitating child centred and activity based learning.

(a) whether the ratio of teaching and non-teaching staff, teaching staff and 
students and total staff to students in Regional Engineering college, Srinagar is much 
higher than the ration in other Regional Engineering Colleges; 
(b) whether the Regional Engineering College, Srinagar did not invest the 
GPF/CPF receipts between Rs.Q/42 crore and Rs. 1.61 crore in long term 
deposits during 1995-2000, which resulted in loss of interest of Rs.54 lakh; 
(c) if so, the reasons for the both; and 
(d) the corrective measures being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
(DR (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) Yes, sir. The ratio of teaching & non-
teaching staff, teaching staff & students and total staff to the students is higher in 
comparison to similar ratio in other Regional Engineering Colleges in the 
country. 
(b) to (d) Yes, sir. The Regional Engineering College, Srinagar did not invest 
the amount under long term deposit due to resources constraint from time to 
time. The Regional Engineering College, Srinagar has been advised to get the 
matter inquired into and take all possible corrective measure to check the 
recurrence of the lapse.

2817. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of a recent survey of Asian Universities, 
conducted by Asia week, a Hong Kong based, English weekly; 
(b) whether Government are also aware that not a single Indian University 
figures among the first twenty universitie s in the list, excep t for JNU, which 
was ranked above fifty in the Asian region; 
332 

[18 December, 2001]       RAJYA SABHA 
(c) what are the reasons for poor standard of Indian Universities; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to upgrade the standards of Indian Universities, to 
bring them at par with foreign Universities of International repute? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (DR, (SHRIMATI) RITA VERM A): (a) to (d) Surveys 
made by periodicals are usually not based on universally accepted parameters 
endorsed by an international body su ch as UNESCO etc. They, therefore, 
have limited value. The Government, however, is fully conscious of the generic 
issue of quality upgradation in higher education. Towards this end, assessment and 
accreditation has now been made obligatory for all universities and colleges. 
Other aspects of a qualitative nature including curricula updating, improving IT 
facilities, induction and inservicc training of teachers, adherence to a minimum 
level of working days and teaching hours arc being focused upon.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) Over the period of last three years a total of 24

approx.) The landed cost of these coaches is Rs. 159 crore (approx.). 
(b) Integral Coach Factory, Chennai and other Indian coach factories have 
so far been manufacturing coaches to the technology imported in the 1950s. 
Though, this technology has been progressively improved to higher speeds 
and better riding characteristics, it has been streched to its limits. As a result, 
the existing coaches have become very maintenace intensive. For any further 
increase in the speed of trains and to run longer trains with improved safety a 
quantum upgradation in technology of coaches was necessary. Indian Railways 
therefore, entered into a transfer of technology cont ract alongwith supply of 
24 coaches with M/s ALSTOM LHB. Germany for building latest technolgy 
coaches in India, Manufacturing capability and expertise for these new type 
of coachs are being developed at Rail Coach Factory, Kapurthala and actual

2837. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether is is a fact that while the world average speed for 
passenger train movement is 300 kmph and freight trains is at 200 
kmph, such speeds in India are placed at 162 kmph and 75 kmph, 
respectively; 
(b) if so, the specific reasons identified for the low average speeds in 
India; and 
(c) the steps being taken to improve these speeds, including the details of 
phased measures contemplated in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (c) Ministry of Railways does not have any 
official record about th e speed potential of frei ght and passenger trains 
operating on foreign railway systems. As per Jane's World Railways 1998-99 
publication, the fastest Highspeed Passenger Trains in the world are normally 
operating in the speed range of 275 to 300 kmph. The maximum speed 
recorded by high speed passenger trains in Japan is between 260—275 kmph. 
In the freight category, the Japanese Railways has Rolling stock capable of 
running at a speed of 130 kmph. 
Indian Railways has capability to run Passenger trains in the speed range of 
130—140 kmph and the goods trains in the speed range of 75—100 kmph. 
The reason for lower speed potential of passenger trains is that Indian 
Railways operate in a mixed traffi c environment, where slow moving 
passenger and goods trains and also fast moving Express trains run on the 
same track. In foreign countries such fast services are run on dedicated track 
with hightly sophisticated equipments. Investments in such services call for 
massive funds in dedicated infrastructure and corresponding maintenance 
facilities. Such ventures 
358

require very high volumes and paying capacity.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER AND DISCUSSION IN CONNECTION 
WITH 
TERRORIST ATTACK ON PARLIAMENT HOUSE ON THE 
13
TH
 DECEMBER, 2001 
THE LEADER OF THE HOU SE AND THE MINISTER OF 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Mr. Chairman, Sir,... 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal) : Sir, we have to 
get copies of the statement. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, it is a legitimate requirement of 
copies in both Hindi and English. As I am making the statement, the 
statement is being replicated and will be here in the House available in 
sufficient copies very shortly. Su re. In the meantime, with your 
permission, Sir, on behalf of my senior colleague, the Home Minister, I 
would like to make the following statement in connection with the 
terrorist attack on Parliament House on 13* December, 2001. 
The ghastly attack on Parliament House on 13 th December, 
2001 has shocked the entire nation. The terrorist assault on the very 
bastion of our democracy was clearly aimed at wiping out the 
country's top political leadership. 
It is a tribute to our security personnel that they rose to the 
occasion and succeeded in averti ng what could have been a national 
catastrophe. In doing so, they made the supreme sacrifice for which 
the country would always remain indebted to them. It is now evident 
that the 
426 

[18 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
terrorists assault on the Parliament  House was executed jointly by 
Pak-based and supported terrorist outfits, namely, Laskar-e-Taiba and 
Jaish-e-Mohammad. These two organisations are known to derive 
their support and patronage from t he Pak I.S.I. The investigation so 
far carried out by the police shows that all the five terrorists, who 
formed a suicide squad, were Paki stani nationals. All of them were 
killed on the spot, and their Indian associates have since been 
nabbed and arrested. The investigation at this stage indicates that the 
five Pakistani terrorists entered the Parliament House Complex at. 
about 11.40 AM in an Ambassador Car, bearing registration No. DL-
3CJ-1527 and moved towards Building Gate No. 12 when it 
encountered the carcade of the Vice -President of India, which was 
parked at Gate No. 11. One of the members of the Parliament House 
Watch and Ward Staff, Shri Ja gdish Prasad Yadav, became 
suspicious about the identity of t he car, and immediately ran after it. 
The car was forced to turn backward, and in the process, it. hit the 
Vice-President's car. When chall enged by the security personnel 
present on the spot, all the five terrorists jumped out of the car and 
started firing indiscriminately. The Delhi Police personnel, attached 
with the Vice-President security, as also the personnel of the C.R.P.F. 
and the I.T.B.P. on duty immediately took their positions and returned 
the fire. It was at this point that another member of the Parliament 
House Watch and Ward staff, Shri Matbar Singh, sustained bullet 
injuries. He rushed inside Gate No. 11 and closed it. An alarm was 
raised and all the gates in the building were immediately closed. The 
terrorists ran towards Gate No. 12, and then to Gate No. 1 of the 
Parliament House Building. One terrorist was shot dead by the 
security forces at Gate No. 1, an d in the process, the explosives 
wrapped around his body exploded. The remaining four terrorists 
turned back and reached Gate No. 9 of the Building. Three of them 
were gunned down there. The fifth terrorist ran towards Gate No. 5 
where, he also was gunned down by the SPG personnel. During the 
exchange of fire, four Delhi Police personnel, namely, Shri Nanak 
Chand, Assistant Sub-Inspector, Shri Rampal, Assistant Sub-
Inspector.. Shri Om Prakash, Head Constable, and Shri Ghanshyam, 
Head Constable, attached with the Vice-President's security, lost their 
lives on the spot. The other three persons, who were also killed, were 
Smt. Kamlesh Kumari, a woman constable of C.R.P.F., Shri Jagdish 
Prasad Yadav, a security assistant of the Watch and Ward Staff of the 
Parliament House, who had rushed after the terrorists' car, and a 
civilian employee of the C.P.W.D., Shri Desh Raj. 
427 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December, 2001] 
Eighteen other persons were injured and they were immediately 
rushed to Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital for medical treatment. These 
included Shri Matbar Singh, Security Assistant, Watch & Ward Staff of the 
Parliament House, who later succumbed to his injuries. The scene of the 
crime was cordoned off and Investigation Teams, including Forensic 
Experts and Bomb Detection Squads, were pressed into service. A number 
of hand grenades were recovered from the site of the incident and defused. 
A large quantity of arms and ammunition, including explosives, was also 
recovered. 
The breakthrough in the investigation of the case was 
achieved with the arrest of Syed Abdul Rehman Geelani, a Lecturer in a 
local college, whose interrogation led to the identification of two other 
accomplices, Afzal and Shaukat Hussain Guru. The wife of the latter 
disclosed that her husband and Afzal had, in the afternoon of 13*" 
December, left for Srinagar. This information was immediately conveyed 
to the Jammu and Kashmir Police who apprehended both of them. A 
laptop computer and Rs. 10 lakhs in cash was recovered from them. 
They were later brought to Delhi by a Special Team deputed for the 
purpose by the Delhi Police. 
Interrogation of the accused persons has revealed that Afzal 
was the main coordinator, who was assigned the task by a Pakistani 
national, Gazi Baba of Jaish-e-Mohammed. Afzal had earlier been 
trained in a camp run by Pak-lSl at Muzaffarabad in Pak-occupied 
Kashmir. The hideouts for the five Pak terrorists were arranged by 
Shaukat Hussan Guru, two in Mukherjee Nagar and one in Timarpur 
area in North Delhi. During the subsequent raids, the Police recovered 
from two of these hideouts a large quantity of Ammonium Nitrate and 
other ingredients used in preparing Improvised Explosive Devices, a map 
of Delhi, a sheet of paper carrying a map of Chanakyapuri, drawn in hand, 
and three police uniforms. 
This incident once again established that terrorism in India is the 
handiwork of Pakistan-based terrorist outfits, known to derive their support 
and sustenance from Pak-ISI. The hijacking of IC-814 Flight to 
Kandahar, the terrorist intrusion into the Red Fort, and the attack on J & K 
Legislative Assembly Complex at Srinagar on 1* October, this year, were 
masterminded and executed by militant outfits, at the behest of the ISI. 
Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed, in particular, have been in 
the forefront in organising terrorist violence in the country. The 
Pakistan High Commissioner in India was summoned to the Ministry of 
External Affairs and 
428 

[18 December. 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
issued a verbal demarche, demanding that Islamabad take action 
against the two terrorist outfits involved in the afack on the Parliament 
House. 
Last week's attack on Parliament is undoubtedly the most 
audacious, and also the most alarming, act of terrorism in the nearly two-
decades-long history of Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in India. This 
time, the terrorists, and their mentors across the border, had the temerity to 
try to wipe out the entire political leadership of India, as represented in our 
multiparty Parliament. 
Naturally, it is time for all of us in this august House, and all of 
us in the country, to ponder why the terrorists and their backers tried to 
raise the stakes so high, particularly, at a time when Pakistan is claiming 
to be a part of the international coalition against terrorism. 
The only answer that satisfactorily addresses this query is that 
Pakistan-itself a product of the indefensible Two-Nation Theory; itself a 
theocratic State with an extremely tenuous tradition of democracy-is 
unable to reconcile itself with the r eality of secular, democratic, self-
confident and steadily progressing India, whose standing in the international 
community is getting inexorably higher, with the passage of time. 
The Prime Minister, in his address to the nation on 13th December, 
2001, has declared that the fight against terrorism had reached a decisive 
phase. The supreme sacrifice made by the security personnel, who 
lost their lives in this incident, will not be allowed to go in vain. Those 
behind the attack on Parliament House should know that the Indian 
people are united and determined to stamp out terrorism from the 
country.  Thank you. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Mr. Chairman, I thank the 
hon. Minister of External Affairs and the Leader of the House for the 
statement that he has made. Most of the facts stated by him in this 
statement have already appeared in the Press. Our party joins all our 
countrymen In condemning the dastardly terrorist attack on Parliament on 
13th December. Parliament is the heart and the nerve centre of our 
democracy and that is, probably, the reason why this terrorist gang tried to 
strike at the citadel of democracy, that is, our Parliament. 
429 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December. 2001]  
Sir, our party is one with the nation in its solemn resolve that we 
shall not make any compromises with these terrorist gangs. We shall pay 
whatever price is necessary to wipe out terrorism, and we are sure that our 
nation will prevail in this regard. 
Sir, on this occasion, our thoughts, our minds and our hearts go to 
those brave security personnel and members of the Watch and Ward 
Staff of our Parliament, who, in an act of supreme sacrifice, in an act of 
supreme devotion to their duty, laid down their lives to save the honour and 
dignity of this august House. Our sympathies go to the members of the 
bereaved families; to those who have suffered injuries, we wish them 
speedy recovery. 
Mr. Chairman, this is not an occasion to apportion blame or find 
fault with our system, w hether it is of intelligence or of security 
arrangements. Yet, it is a fact that  an attack on Parliament was quite 
anticipated. As early as on the 5th of this month, the hon. Home Minister, 
speaking at a meeting of the Feder ation of Indian Chambers of 
Commerce and Industry, had alluded to this threat to our Parliament. 
In fact, one day before this attack took place, i.e. on I2 m 
December, while speaking at Mumbai, the hon. Prime Minister himself 
had referred to the existence of this threat, such a threat to our Parliament. 
Subsequently, we have also learnt t hat the Maharashtra police, while 
interrogating a suspect Al-Qaeda member, Afroz in Mumbai informed the 
Central Government of the plans of this outfit to attack the Parliament. I 
have been told that the Maharashtra Government had informed the 
Central Government about what Afroz had told them. I have also been 
tdd that a member of the IB was also associated with the interrogation of 
Afroz. 
Sir, that despite these advance warnings this daring and dastardly 
attack took place should make all of us sit back and reflect on the 
adequacy of our security and intelligence arrangements. The hon. Home 
Minister, some days ago, had publicly stated that there was no security 
breach. Yet, it is a fact that a car wi th terrorists armed to the teeth was 
allowed to roam about in the high security zone and pass through the 
outer gate and enter the compound of our Parliament. Obviously, the 
checks being conducted on vehicles need to be tightened much further 
and these checks have to be thorough. It is also clear that the terrorists 
have the support of a well-knit organisation.   The identity of the 
organisational 
430 

[18 December. 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
support bases and the networks that sustain these terrorist organisations 
ought to be diligently explored and exposed with actual facts. Naturally, the 
question arises, "What do we do in the face of this daring and dastardly 
attack?" Certainly, the nation's sentiments have been aroused. I believe, 
it was Jawaharla! Nehru who once said in a letter addressed to his 
daughter, late Shrimati Indira Gandhi, "In affairs of State, while one should 
be full of sentiments, one should nev er be sentimental". Therefore, we 
have to be coot-headed in formulating our response. We should avoid a 
tired and superfluous jingoism. Acting in self-defence is, of course, an 
inherent right of any sovereign nation sanctified by the United Nations 
Charter. But, Sir, before taking any action we must ponder over the 
consequences of alternative courses of action and the trade-offs that 
may exist. First and foremost, we should marshal all our available 
information and convince the members of the international community 
about the evil designs of cross-border terrorism of a most vicious type 
which have sought to attack the heart of our democracy. The hon. 
Minister of External Affairs has pointed out the role of the ISI at the back 
of all these operations and I believe we should marshal all this evidence 
and convince the members of the international community that what is 
applicable in dealing with the terrorists in Afghanistan must be applicable 
to these terrorists also who have perpetrated such a ghastly act on the 
Indian territory. 
Sir, I was, in this context, disturbed about the statement which 
appeared in the Press; I am mentioning about the statement of the 
Secretary of State of the United States calling 'India for restraint' and 
going on to say that General Musharraf was taking all possible steps that 
were necessary. I would like to know from the hon. External Affairs Minister 
as to what in his assessment is of the attitude of the United States and 
other Members of the international community towards this latest ghastly 
act perpetrated by terrorist gangs inspired, aided and abetted by 
Pakistan. Obviously, we have, on the diplomatic front, a lot more to do. 
Sir, furthermore, a question arises about the action that we 
ought to take. Any action that we take, in our view, must be effective 
and sustainable. Loose talk of attacking terrorist bases or hot pursuit must 
give way to a sober analysis of political and military consequences of 
various options open to us. In this context, it is also highly important that 
the Government take the Opposition into confidence. We are one with 
the Government in re-affirming that our nation will prevail, shall prevail, 
over the 
431 

RAJYA SABHA [18 December. 2001]  
evil designs pf terrorists. Any well-considered action, taking into account, its 
viability and sustainability, after careful consideration of its long and short-term 
consequences will have our support. But the Government has an obligation to 
take the Opppsitipn intp ccnfidence.  Thank you, Sir.

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I join the entire 
nation in condemning this dastardly act, which took place on December 13, on 
the vital institution of democracy, wh ich is the biggest in the world. I 
congratulate and salute the valour  and the courage that has been 
demonstrated by our security forces who have made supreme sacrifices in 
protecting the lives of the people who were inside the Parliament, and my 
Party joins the entire nation in extending our sympathies to the members of 
the bereaved families. 
Sir, one vital point is that this issu e, the issue of terrorism, the threat 
to the integrity of the nation, has  been discussed earlier also. This  issue has 
been discussed very exhaustively. I am very happy that the main Opposition 
parties-there were, earlie r, some different view s which I read in the 
newspapers-are extending their cooperation. I offer my thanks to at least 
those parties who have given unstinte d cooperation, giving an impression to 
the entire world that India is one in fighting terrorism or in solving any national 
crisis or problem. Sir, this is not the time to score points against each other; 
this is not the time to make political capital out of the events. Sir, whenever a 
national crisis is there, people are united, but, unfortunately, political parties try 
to take advantage of it. By sensing the mood of the people, they are being 
guided. This is my observation; that has been happening. 
Sir, I read in the newspapers that, immediately after this incident, the 
resignations of the Prime Minister, the Defence Minister and the Home

Minister had been demanded,. Sir, when a similar incident took place in the 
United States, when the World Trade Centre was attacked, none had 
demanded the resignation of Mr. Bush; the entire country rallied behind him - 
that was the strength - in  solving the problem. At least now, wisdom has 
prevailed, and I am very happy, Sir, to note from the trend of the deliberations 
that are being taking place in this august House that the Members have not 
minced words in expressing their views. That is giving an impression that the 
country is united, the countr y is one, the entire nation is one, in solving this 
crisis. 
Sir, I appreciate the courage shown by the hon. Prime Minister and 
the Defence Minister who had gone round the Parliament House and tried to 
boost the morale of the people. Sir, it  may be irrelevant for certain persons.

America, the President of the United St ates of America was taken to a safer

The Vice-President was not to be seen for more than a week. 
Therefore, I really appreciate t he courage and prudence that has been 
exhibited by our hon. Prime Minister. 
Here, I would like to have a clarification from the hon. Minister. What 
is the attitude of the Unit ed States with regard to the cross-border terrorism 
that we are facing in this country? When such an incident took place in the 
United States, we were the first to react. We had extended all support. We 
had announced that we would become a partner of the alliance in fighting 
terrorism. I don't think the United States will have different yardsticks for 
measuring terrorism in India and in the United States. In the last session, 
when a discussion took place on terrorism, I made a suggestion to the hon. 
Minister: "Why can't you utilise our good offices with the United States to 
influence Pakistan, which is breeding terrorist camps, through the ISI, by 
financing and arming them?" The reply was that a mighty nation like India 
could solve its own problem without approaching the US. I request the hon. 
Foreign Minister to, at least, emulate the example of Mr. George Bush who 
could rally the entire world behind him,  in spite of Islamic fundamentalism. 
This is a vital point that I want to  make. The Talibans or the Pakistanis, 
whoever they may be, want to personify the fight against Taliban as a fight 
against Islam. Fortunately, they could not succeed  in  it.     Otherwise,  things 
would  have become very  dangerous

initiatives and make every nation rally behind us, because it is a cause for 
which we have been fighting and to wh ich the other nations had also 
subscribed earlier. Reference has been made to the Powell's statement. It is 
true that they have been advising us to exercise restraint. We are exercising

DR. L.M. SINGHVI (Rajasthan): Madam, "may I first of all pay my 
tribute to those who fell victims to the dastardly attack on the Parliament 
House? They deserve our deepest grat itude and they deserve the greatest 
praise. They lived the lives of very brave persons and they died as very brave 
individuals. I think it is well to say that such dedicated persons who are deeply 
devoted to their duty, like the security staff and the Watch and Ward of 
Parliament, create that faith which is im portant. It was their faith in the nation 
and their sense of duty which inspired them to make the supreme sacrifice of 
their lives in a battle, in a war against terrorism. We can make no mistake that 
those martyrs died in our battle against terrorism in India. Terrorism has, in 
fact, engaged itself in many such skirmishes and battles; but, now, with their 
attack on Parliament House, they appear to have declared their war on India 
and Indian democracy. And this declaration of war on Indian democracy is 
something which all of us must fight together and with a total sense of 
solidarity. That is why I thought it was a welcome occasion to make a common 
cause, to make certain that we speak in unison, with our views orchestrated in 
solidarity, and we may then forge those strong ties in speaking politically 
amongst ourselves and to the world be more able and strong to fight the battle 
against terrorism. In these two decades, we have faced many battles against 
terrorism; in these battles, we have faced them, more or less, single-handed, 
as a nation. The nm September attack on the twin Towers, I had hoped, would 
make a difference, at least in terms of converts KJ India's war against terrorism 
into a global war against terrorism. That is what we understood the message 
of President Bush to be.   I hope that this attack on the Parliament of India will

Power tariff rationalization 
*410. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) what steps have been taken for rationalization of power tariff in Andhra 
Pradesh, Maharashtra and Kamataka in the context of agitations against high power 
tariffs in Andhra and other States, through Central Electricity Regulatory Commission 
or State Electricity Regulatory Commission or otherwise; and 
(b) whether State Electricity Regulatory Commissions have been set up in 
these States, if so, the composition and functions thereof and if not, in which States 
steps are being taken to set up State Commissions? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) and (b) The 
Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) Act, 1998 has paved way for 
establishment of Regulatory Commission at the Centre and the State with a view 
to rationalisation of electricity tariff, transparent policies .regarding subsidies, 
etc. Under the provisions of this Act, the Central Government has constituted the 
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC). Maharashtra has 
constituted State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) under the ERC Act, 
1998 while Andhra Pradesh and Kamataka have constituted SERCs under their 
respective State Reform Acts. The SERCs in all these three States consist of three 
Members including Chairperson. Sixteen other States have also constituted SERCs. 
So far 11 State Commissions have issued tariff orders. 
CERC has been entrusted with the powers inter alia to determine tariff for 
Central Generating Companies and inter-State Transmission Companies etc., while 
SERCs have been given power inter alia to determine tariff for electricity, wholesale, 
bulk, grid or retails as the case may be within the State. 
Under the ERC Act, 1998 the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions, 
while fixing tariff are to be guided by the principle that tariff progressively reflects 
the cost of supply of electricity at an adequate and improving level of efficiency 
and if the State Governments so desires it can grant subsidy to any consumer or 
class of consumers in the tariff determined by SERC by paying the amount to 
compensate the utility affected by grant of such subsidy. 
Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (APERC) announced its 
first tariff order which was made effective in June, 2000. There had been an 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
average tariff increase of 15%. The tariff order sought to reduce cross subsidy and 
link tariffs to cost of service. For domestic consumers average tariff was increased 
by 54%. However, to mitigate the impact of tariff increase on residential 
consumers, the Government provided additional subsidy of Rs. 281 crore. Total 
subsidy paid by .the Government of Andhra Pradesh during 2000-01 is Rs. 1626 
crore. The APERC has issued second tariff order on 24.3.2001 proposing no tariff 
hike for the year 2001-02 except minor adjustment of tariff for domestic consumers. 
Government of Andhra Pradesh has committed subsidy of Rs. 1561.41 crores 
during 2001 -02. 
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) in its first Tariff Order 
dated 5th May, 2000, has directed that the tariff for ail categories would be 
simplified and would be gradually moved towards cost of supply. In tariff proposal 
for 2001-02 in the pursuance of MERC's order, MSEB has tried to rationalize the 
tariff by reducing 40 Nos. of categories/tariff rates to 17 Nos. Also subsidy 
deviation from cost of supply which was between 30% to 141% has been brought 
down to 38% to 125%. 
Kamataka Electricity Regulatory Commission (KERC) has issued its first 
tariff order which has made effective from 29th December, 2000. The average tariff 
increase was equivalent to about 17% as against the hike of 24.5% proposed by 
Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. (KPTCL). Government of 
Kamataka have agreed to give an additional subsidy of Rs. 144 crore to give relief to 
agricultural consumers below 10 Horse Power (HP).

The need was felt in 1985 for an autopilot for incorporation into the Jaguar

were available and a decision was taken to install the autopilot. A contract was

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRICHENNAMANENIVIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The State Government of Jammu and Kashmir has informed that, on 
22.11.2001, a raid was conducted on the residential house of one Gh. Mohammad Dar 
s/o Mohammad Abdullah Dar R/o Safakadal, Srinagar on the basis on an intelligence 
input that terrorists had established a hide-out in the said house. During the 
operation, a substantial quantity of arms/ammunition, explosives, etc. were recovered

13 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
Invoking the provisions of the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance, 2001 (POTO), a case 
FIR No. 218/2001 was registered at Police Station, Safakadal (Srinagar). The house 
in question was sealed as the initial investigation led to the belief that the hide-out had 
been constructed out of the proceeds of terrorism. Upon a further legal examination 
of the issue, it was found that only a part of the house, being used as a hide-out of 
terrorists, could be reasonably believed to have been constructed out of the 
proceeds of terrorism and not the entire house. It was, therefore, decided that the 
seizure of the house was not warranted in this case and the house was accordingly 
restored to the family.

Reforms in mining sector 
3044. SHRISOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
COAL AND MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a proposal under active consideration of the Union 
Government to introduce reforms in mining sector/coal mining sector to effect 
a major change during the Tenth Plan period; 
(b) if so, the details thereof in all respects; 
(c) when the reforms are expected to be initiated; and 
(d) how far it shall improve the mining conditions/coal production and 
reduction in prices thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL AND MINES 
(SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (c) The major reforms initiatives are 
as follows: 
1. The Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 2000 has been 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha with the following objectives: 
(i)   To allow the Indian Companies to mine coal and lignite in the country 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
without the existing restriction of captive mining. In other words, the 
objective is to allow the Indian companies in public and private sector 
to mine coal and lignite and also to sell the same in the open market. 
(ii)   To allow the Indian Companies in the public and private sector to be 
engaged in exploration of coal and lignite resources in the country. 
The purpose is to augment production of coal in the country through 
association of the private sector with the existing nationalised coal sector to 
bridge the demand and supply gap assessed for the Xth and Xlth plan period. 
2. Recently the Government have revised the coal mining policy of 1979 
spelling out the conditions under which the State Government undertakings 
can do coal mining. Under the revised policy, the State Government companies 
or undertakings are allowed to do mining of coking and non-cocking coal or 
lignite reserves, either by opencast or underground method, anywhere in the 
country. 
3. The Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 which 
govern the mining sector including coal and lignite, was last amended in 
December 1999 and subsequently two principal Rules, viz, Mineral Concession 
Rules, 1960 and Mineral Conservation & Development Rule, 1988 have been 
amended thrice in a bid to simplify the procedure for grant of mineral concession, 
to attract more and more foreign direct  investment in mining sector and to 
delegate more and more powers to the State Governments, who are the owners 
of the minerals. Therefore, reforms in mining and coal sector is an ongoing 
process. Total number of Foreign Investment Promotion Board's (FIPB) approval 
in the mining sector is 70; the foreign equity component of the approval is 
approximately Rs. 4,000 crores. 
4. Two Working Groups-one on Mineral Exploration and the other on 
Coal and Lignite-were constituted by the Planning Commission to make 
recommendations for the Tenth Five Year Plan. The two Working Groups have 
submitted their reports to the Planning Commission. 
(d) Reforms should attract higher investment, better technology and more 
skilled manpower should foster competition and better management practices; 
should keep the domestic mining sector to face international competition; and 
above all; should promote delivery of better products and services at more 
competitive prices to the consumers.

projects/schemes for the rescue and rehabilitation of women and children affected 
by the flesh trade either through their own agencies or in collaboration with

under the Central Government in case of direct recruitment on all India basis 
by open competition is 15 per cent and 7.5 per cent respectively. In case of direct 
recruitment on all India basis otherwise than by open competition reservation 
for SCs and STs is respectively 16.66 per cent and 7.5 per cent. In case of direct

locality or a region, percentage of reservation for SCs and STs is generally fixed

for STs, provided the element of direct  recruitment, if any, does not exceed 
75 per cent.

OBCs in services under the Government of India is already 49.5 per cent and 
50 per cent in case of direct recruitment on all India basis by open competition 
and on all India basis otherwise than by open competition respectively. Under 
the circumstances revising the percentage of reservation for Scheduled Castes 
and Scheduled Tribes as per their population, is neither contemplated under 
Article 16(4) of the Constitution nor feasible, as such revision would make the 
total reservation for SCs/STs and OBCs in excess of 50 per cent. 
Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Bill, 2000 was introduced in the 
Lok Sabha on 27.11.2000, seeking to extend the existing constitutional embargo 
on undertaking fresh delimitation of electoral constituencies upto the year 2026 
AD and simultaneously to undertake readjustment and rationalization of 
constituencies in the States, without altering the number of seats allotted to 
each State in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies of the States, 
including the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribe constituencies, on the 
basis of the population ascertained at the census for the year 1991 as also to re fix 
the number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes 
in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies of the States on the basis 
of the population ascertained at the census for the year 1991, was passed by the 
Lok Sabha on 21.8.2001 and by the Rajya Sabha on 23.82001. The said Bill is now 
in the process of being ratified by the State Legislatures before receiving the 
assent of the President under the provisions of the Article 368 of the Constitution. 
Pursuant to its enactment the Government will further bring a legislation which 
will provide for setting up of an authority to carry out the purposes of the 
aforesaid Constitution Amendment Bill. 
As regards reservation of seats in the PanchayatsTthe same is governed 
by Article 243 D (1) of the Constitution of India.

(SHRI l.D. SWAMI): (a) and (b) There is no Special Cell in the Ministry of Home

1996 1892

'Police' and 'Public Order' are State subjects as per Seventh Schedule to 
the Constitution of India. As such, registration, investigation, detection and 
prevention of crime is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments. 
However, the Central Government has been adivising the State Governments, 
from time to time, to give more focussed attention to the improvement of 
administration of Criminal Justice System. Information relating to the busting of 
immigration rackets by the local police is not maintained centrally. 
Improvements in the security features of Indian Passports and Visa stickers 
to minimize tampering are undertaken on a continuing basis. All immigration 
staff also exercise vigilance in this regard and are given special training and 
equipment to scrutinize travel documents to ascertain their genuineness. New 
security features in the passport are introduced from time to time to make them 
tamper proof. 
(c) and (d) No formal study has been carried out by the Central 
Government. However, it has come to the notice of the Government that the 
modus operandi adopted by illegal immigrants traveling on forged passports 
includes departure from Kathmandu or smaller airports in India being used for 
international travel. Many countries including Cyprus, Malta and Thailand 
provide visa on arrival. Many illegal migrants prefer to proceed to these countries 
first and then target some other countries. A number of them also use complicated 
routes through several countries using a combination of land and air passage 
and purchasing documents along the way.

Solar Energy Powered Air Quality Monitoring Station at Agra 
3122. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister, of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court has di rected the Ministry to make 
arrangements to run air quality monitoring station in Agra with solar energy to 
protect the Taj from pollution; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) would Government consider the same arrangement for other national 
monuments to protect them from pollution? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRIM. KANNAPPAN): (a) and (b) To 
monitor the pollution level in the Taj Mahal complex, the Archaeological Survey 
of India (ASI) and the UP Pollution Control Board (UPPCB) have installed air 
quality monitoring stations. In view of erratic power supply, these agencies 
have been using diesel generating sets as back up power source to operate the 
equipment of air quality monitoring stations. 
The Supreme Court in course of hearing a petition relating to impact of air 
pollution on the Taj Mahal, has directed the ASI, the Central Pollution Control 
Board and the UPPCB vide its order dated 27th November, 2001 to instal solar 
energy systems to power the air quality monitoring stations in four months 
time. The Court has also directed that for the time being the Central Government 
should meet the cost of using this technology. 
(c) The Ministry has also informed the Court that it can provide technical 
support to the ASI to study the feasibility of using solar photovoltaic systems 
in other protected monuments. The ASI has no such plan under their

New Policy regarding captive power plants 
3134. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA : Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether a new policy regarding captive power plants has been drafted 
to facilitate full utilization of installed capacity of these plants; and 
(b) if so, the progress on the finalization of this policy? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYA WANTIMEHTA) :(a) and (b) The State Governments have been requested 
to encourage setting up of captive generations mechanism plants and to create 
an institutional mechanism which may allow captive power units an easy entry 
into the power sector by quickly clearing captive power applications, giving the 
developers a rational tariff for purchase of surplus power by the grid and third 
party access for direct sale of power to other industrial units. Under Secton 44 
of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, the State Electricity Boards (SEBs) given 
consent to setting up of captive power plants by various industries irrespective 
of the capacity of such plants. Consultation of Central Electricity Authority is 
necessary only in cases where the captive power project exceeds 25 MW. 
On July 11, 2001 the Minister of Power has circulated a Captive Power 
Policy prepared by the Ministry of Power in consultation with the CEA to all the 
State Governments and Union Territories. In this policy, the following has been 
included: 
• If captive plant is of Hydro or cogeneration, such plant, irrespective of 
its size, may be permitted liberally. 
• If captive power plant is based on coal or liquid fuel or gas such plant 
may be allowed and capacity of the plant permitted upto 200% of the 
requirement of industry (If the state is deficit in power). 
• Captive power plant may be allowed if State/SEB or successor entity 
are unable to supply the required power supply. Such a captive power 
plant can be considered for the uninterrupted power supply to the 
industry even if the State is surplus in power. 
• If the industry required quality power supply which is not available, 
the proposal for installation of  the captive power plant can be 
considered. 
• If the cost of generation from captive power plant is found to be lower, 
the proposal may be considered after examining the cost and tariff. 
• Units in Special Economic Zone (SEZs) and industrial entities may be 
allowed to set up captive power plants liberally. 
• Bank facilities are propose to be provided to CPPs. The rates for banking 
may be determined on mutualy agreed terms. 
106 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
•   Prior approval of SEB has to be obtained for wheeling of power. 
Wheeling may be done to any service (HT or LT). Wheeling charges 
may be worked out based on pooled rates worked out by Central/State 
Transmission Utility of that region. 
• The tariff for sale of power from thermal and hydro CPPs, may be fixed

Constitution of National Land Use and Wasteland Development Council 
3152. SHRISOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether "National Land Use and Wasteland Development Council" 
has been constituted; 
(b) if so, when and the names of persons in the council and the term of the 
council; 
(c) how many meetings have been held with dates; and 
(d) the decisions taken for expediting Wasteland Development 
Programme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PAT1L): (a) to (d) The Ministry of 
Environment & Forests, Government of India had set up a National Land Use 
and Wastelands Development Council headed by the Prime Minister with Chief 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
Ministers of all the States/Union Territori es, Ministers/Ministers of States of 
certain Central Ministries/Departments, Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission, 
Chairman of National Land Use & Conservation Board and Chairman of National 
Wastelands Development Board as Members in May, 1985. The Council was set 
up as the highest policy planning and coordinating agency for all issues 
concerning the health and scientific management of the country's land resources. 
It does not have any fixed term and has only ex-qfficio Members, as indicated 
above. The Council has held only one meeting on 6.2.1986 and the decisions 
taken, relating to Wastelands Development, at this meeting, are given in the 
statement. 
Statement 
Decisions taken at the first meeting of the National Land Use and 
Wastelands Development Council held on 6.2.1986 relating to 
Wastelands Development 
1.     Identification of Wastelands 
1.1  The State Governments should id entify wastelands in forest areas, 
revenue common land or degraded farm land. 
12    At least 5% and 20% of these wastelands should be utilised in 1986-
87 and in the Seventh Five Year Plan respectively for afforestation, 
development of pasture and forest-based industries. 
2    Nodal Agency 
A nodal agency/mechanism should be  created in the State for (a) 
coordinating, funding and activities re lating to different schemes of 
afforestation and wastelands development; and (b) for monitoring and 
evaluation of the various schemes. 
3. State Seeds Corporation 
The work of the State Seeds Corporation should be extended to include 
the production and supply of fodder, grasses and legume seeds on a 
commercial basis to farmers. 
4. Direct Seeding 
4.1 Seeds, suitably pelletised, to enable the retention of mulches and 
hydrogels, should be distributed to growers with suitable instructions 
for sowing. 
124 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
4.2    In remote and difficult areas, in critical watersheds and ravines, aerial 
seeding must be considered. 
5. Leasing of Land 
The State Government must lay down clear guidelines for the leasing 
of forest and non-forest wastelands to the rural poor. 
6. Urban Fuel wood and Green Belts  
The State must set up a machinery for providing a green belt of fuelwood 
and fodder plantations around towns and cities. 
7. Degraded Forest Areas 
7.1 The State Forest Department must identify degraded scrub forest land 
which must be broadcast with fodder and legume seeds, so that the 
resultant fodder may be used by the local people, keeping in view that 
an estimated one million hectares of scrub forests in the country is to 
be brought back to green cover each year. 
7.2 Degraded forest area must be used to raise fuelwood plantations to 
provide for the use of the local community, through their involvement. 
8. Forest Development Corporations 
The State Forest Development Corporation must not confine itself to 
exploitation of forest produce. Fuelwood and fodder plantations, both 
within the degraded forest area and in wastelands outside, must be 
actively undertaken by the Forest Development Corporation with the 
help of institutional finance. 
9. Forest-Based Industries 
9.1 Forest-based industries should not only be encouraged to afforest 
wastelands with a view to secure  raw material but also make a 
commitment to undertake fuelwood and fodder plantations for the use 
of local communities on a part of the land leased to them. 
9.2 Industries must also enter into agreements with small farmers for the 
supply of their raw material needs on a viable basis. 
9.3 Such plantations must be raised on wastelands distant from habitations, 
so as not to disturb existing community use. 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
10. Government Department/Public Sector Undertakings of the States 
and Central Governments 
10.1 Government departments/undertakings in possession of substantial 
areas of unutilised land in their control, should cover these areas with 
tree/fodder cover. 
10.2 Railway sides, road sides and canal sides must also be afforested at the 
cost of the Departments concerne d, who should provide a specific 
allocation therefor. 
11. People's Involvement 
11.1 Nurseries: The social forestry programmes should lay greater emphasis 
on people's involvement through nursery relating and farm forestry. 
By 1987-88, at least 50% of the total seedings in each State should be 
raised through people's nurseries, i.e., kisans, schools, women and 
youth groups. Further, such nurseries should also be specially 
decentralised so that a nursery is available within a 10 km. radius. 
11.2 Sapling Distribution: A uniform policy of distribution of sapling at a 
minimum price of 10 to 20 paise should be considered, the prices 
being gradually increased to its real value. It must be recognised that 
free distribution is counterproductiv e to emergence of free market 
operations in sale of saplings. 
11.3 Farm Forestry: Farmers should be encouraged to plant saplings on 
their field-bunds or farms. 
 
11.4 Tree Grower's Cooperatives: Tree Grower's Cooperatives must be 
promoted which should provide inputs and technical guidance and 
also make arrangements for harvesting and marketing. 
11.5 Tree Pattas: The State must formulate a Tree Patta Scheme, wherever 
such a scheme is not already in fo rce. A specific target for the year 
must be prescribed and achieved. 
11.6 Strip Plantations: The State Government must consider introducing a 
tree patta scheme for lessing given strips of land for plantation on 
roadside and canalside. 
11.7 The State Government must simp lify the procedure for the Tree Patta 
Scheme. 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
12. Media and Communications 
A massive campaign must be launched to involve the people in 
afforestation and wastelands development. Pamphlets and posters may 
be issued and distributed through Panchayats and Block Development 
Officers on how to raise nurseries, select species, get land lease, get 
bank finance etc. The need is to use all available and possible media 
to make it a people's movement. 
13. Akashvani and Doordarshan 
Akashvani and Doordarshan must develop suitable programmes to 
be broadcast on a regular basis and involve public figures in 
spreading the message.  
14.    School Curriculum 
The curriculum of the schools should include a better understanding 
of land resources, causes of its de gradation wastelands development 
and afforestation. 
15. Monitoring and Evaluation 
Effective steps need to be taken to strengthen the database on which 
policy formulation and monitoring and evaluation of programmes 
can be undertaken. 
16. Remote Sensing Applications Centre 
Remote Sensing Applications Centres must be established in the State, 
wherever not in existence already,  to provide data on resources — 
land, water, mineral, trees, etc. Su ch data may be computerised for 
easy storage and retrieval. 
17. Funds 
All possible ways and means must be exploited — including avenues 
of institutional finance — for the afforestation programme.  
18. Laws 
All Acts relating to planting and harvesting of trees, leasing of land, 
Usufruct Rights, etc. should be examined in the context of amendments 
that may be called for to motivate the rural poor and other institutions 
for afforestation. 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
19.     Role of Government Departments. 
19.1   Policies need to be formulated and enforced so that those who are held 
responsible for degradation and wh o contribute to the increase of 
wastelands are held accountable for re-foresting the degraded lands. 
19.2  Irrigation projects, mining, hydro-electric projects etc. must be 
considered only if sufficient safeguards are built in so that no new 
wastelands are created. Wherever th is is not feasible, compensatory 
afforestation of wastelands must be undertaken by such Projects.

Statement-III 
Recommendations of the study report on consolidation of land 
holdings 
• The scheme of consolidation of land holdings should be formulated 
with reference to uniformity of soil conditions, farm infrastructure, spatial 
features, cropping partem and perceptions on the market value of the 
land specific to each State in a participatory manner. 
• The Policy should address the in stitutional issues like credit, 
technology, marketing, extension and managerial support to the farmers 
accepting the scheme of consolidation of land holdings. 
• The consolidation of land holdings is to be considered as a State subject 
and there is need to organize the State resources to implement the 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
scheme. The central schemes with financial support need not be called 
for to implement the scheme on consolidation of land holdings in various 
States. 
• The States need to formulate regi on specific approaches for the 
consolidation process and should use bottom-up strategies taking the 
concurrence of the farmers. 
• The Panchayats or the local bodies in the State may be empowered to 
implement such schemes. 
• Cooperative farming practices for pooling the land of small and 
marginal farmers need to be en couraged for the commercial and 
horticultural crops as an alternative to the consolidation of land 
holdings. 
• The cooperative farming also manifests largely the objectives of the 
consolidation of land holdings and need to be encouraged wherever 
possible as an alternative to the consolidation of land holding scheme. 
• The success stories of the cooperative farming may be studied and the 
farmers may be motivated for such  experiments for better yield and 
income through the land. 
• There is a strong feeling amongst the farmers that the consolidation 
officers do not take the concurrence of the farmers before confirming 
the scheme and such actions resulted in resistance among the farmers 
to accept the scheme. The concurrence of the farmers on the scheme 
before confirmation needs to be sought in the Gram Sabha. 
• The capacity building exercise need s to be taken up by the Central 
Government for the State Departments chosen to implement the 
sponsored schemes. 
• Confidence needs to be built among the farmers who were already 
covered in the consolidation scheme in some States and are now 
facing post-scheme implementation problems. 
• The scheme of consolidation of land holdings need to be popularized 
among the farmers. 
• The centrally sponsored scheme(s) on consolidation of land holdings 
may be continued in the State on case by case basis assessing their 
132 

[19 December, 2001] RAJYASABHA 
interest in implementing the scheme. Capabilities and competencies in 
delivering the services to the farmers. 
• There is a need to give thorough rethinking on the scheme of 
consolidation of land holdings, as there were many administrative 
and socio-economic hurdles experienced in the past. The scheme may 
be considered on case-by-case basi s in consolidating the wasteland 
for improved agricultural practices. 
• It is necessary to develop some animators from the farmers community 
to generate awareness about the scheme in their peer group. This would 
also help in building strong inter-personal communication base for 
implementation of the Government schemes in the villages. 
• The Gram Sabhas may be used as the platform for disseminating the 
communication on the schemes and their benefits on consolidation of 
land holdings and computerization of land records. 
• The communication campaign may be planned through the interface 
with officials at Gram Sabhas, displaying posters, highlighting success 
stories on consolidation of land holdings and the like. 
Computerization of Land Records 
• The Centrally Sponsored Scheme on the Computerization of Land 
Records has been well received by all the States as they had initiated 
the process of CLR despite some administrative problems. This Scheme 
should continue and all the States need to be covered under this Scheme. 
However, the States may be advise d to meet the recurring costs on 
management of the database. 
• States showing low response like Bihar and Uttar Pradesh may be 
motivated to speed up the work on CLR. There is need for periodical 
intervention of the Government of India to monitor the progress of 
the CLR work, assess the extent of utilization of grants and delivery 
mechanisms to the farmers. 
• The updating of land records by each VAO on schedule needs to be 
encouraged and strict measures have to be imposed thereof. 
• In the process of computerization of land records periodical updating of 
data is a major task and need to perform with all sincerity. This has 
been the major problem at the village and block/tehsil/mandal levels in 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2001 ] 
the States due to administrative reasons. The VAOs are often over-
burdened with variety of responsibilities and could not attend 
satisfactorily to the land records assignments on time. It is suggested 
that the Governments of all States may launch a campaign on updating 
the land records data at the district level during lean agricultural season. 
At least four months in an agriculture year, preferably the lean season 
may be declared as the land records updating period. This could help in 
concentrating on this specific task and complete within scheduled 
period. 
• There is an immediate need for improving computer skilled staff in 
the talukas where there are no operators to manage the systems. There 
are large numbers of vacancies sanctioned by the State Governments 
but they are not yet filled in many States. This is leading to severe 
human resource bottleneck in carrying out the scheme. 
• The compulsory training to the staff at the taluka and district levels 
need to planned for carrying out th e computerization task of land 
records and also the office automation with the existing system 
support. 
• Security measures for the land records data need to be ensured, as it is a 
very sensitive document. The security of the data at the level of 
updating or modification needs to be ensured, as this is absent in all 
the States except in Gujarat. The NI C has to be apprised of this need 
and necessary provisions have to be developed in the package. 
• The data back-ups need to be taken after every update and need to be 
stored in Compact Disks. The use of catridge tape drives (CTD) may 
be gradually replaced by CDs. The co pies of the taluka-wise data in 
CDs need to be kept also at the district level with the office of the 
Superintendent of Land Records or an equivalent competent authority. 
• The maintenance of the systems at the remote places is enormously 
delayed due to accessibility proble m. The companies assigned with 
the annual maintenance contract of the system in a district should be 
asked to appoint resident engineers and sufficient staff for providing 
timely service support. 
• There is need to set-up dial up links with the talukas to the district 
headquarters through networking of the system. The accessibility of 
134 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
the land records data may also be made available to the office of the 
Commissioner Land Records of the State. 
• The linkage needs to be established for on-line data transfer from the Office of 
the Land Registration Authorities in the State/district/taluka to the land reforms 
department, which has taken up the task of computerization of land 
records. Such on-line transfers of land registration would help in up-
dating the land records data faster. 
• The States need to be encouraged to start the process of the delivering 
computerized Record of Rights to the landowners and confidence among the 
farmers about its authenticity and validity need to be developed involving 
concerned officials and local leaders. 
• Presently every State follows its own way of computerization of land records. 
The data variables are different for each State and so the out also is largely 
customized. This is despite the fact that most of them adapt NIC software. 
Consequently, their contents, quality of information and process of 
computerization is amenable to the interstate comparison. Hence there is a 
need for standardizing the format of computerized record of rights across 
the States for developing standardized package of land records. It is 
strongly recommended that a common software need to be developed and 
common variables may also be identified for the record of rights and village 
profile to enable the standardized computing process throughout the country. This 
would help in knowing the right measure and extent of land records in all 
States and maintaining the database. 
The digitization of cadastral maps needs to be done in a more scientific manner 
using appropriate packages. The maps need to be generated in the system by giving 
the scales and not be dependent on the scanning all through the process of digitization. 
There is also a need for updating the survey maps before initiating the digitization 
process in all the States.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI V. 
DHANANJAYA KUMAR): (a) to (c) The Textile Package as announced by the 
Government in the Union Budget for 2000-01 is for the whole country and is not 
State-wise. The provisions regarding duties and taxes contained in the package 
are in implementation with effect from the date on which the Budget came into 
force. The Package is meant to stimulat e the growth of and investment in the 
textile industry. The Package include s duty concession and reliefs, higher 
allocation to important schemes and the announcement of new programmes. 
The main points include—  
• Reduction in the basic customs duty on specified textile machines

the weaving, processing and garment sectors.

of Integrated Apparel Parks to enable dereserved readymade garment 
industry to come up with modem units with the best infrastructure; 
• Emphasising funding from the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme 
for at least 50,000 shuttleless new looms and modernization of 2.5 lakh 
plain looms to automatic looms by 2004; 
• Enhancement of allocation under Technology Upgradation Fund 
Scheme to Rs. 2200 crore from Rs. 50 crore prevailing then; 
• Substantial increase in the Budget allocation for the Ministry of 
Textiles from Rs. 457 crore in 2000-01 to Rs. 650 crore in 2001-02.

situation is such that one cannot be acrimonious on the issues concerned. But, 
I think, it is a very sad state of affa irs that after the statement of the hon. 
Minister and after the interventions of some of the leading Members of the 
Treasury Benches on some of the issues, we are left with a greater sense of 
confusion than clarity. T herefore, what, I think, ought to be discussed by the 
Parliament today is I am not going to  repeat what my le ader and colleague, 
Shri Ramachandran PiHai, has already stated the question of unity. I go back 
to the Resolution which both these Houses adopted on Friday.There were

down their lives and we also

Madam, first of all, I consider it a great privilege to participate in this 
discussion. It comes at a sorrowful moment of the history of this country, when 
the sovereignty of this country itself has been attacked. Terrorism is a virus for 
which there is no medicine. Unless we get rid of terrorism, terrorism will get rid 
of us. It is with that understanding that  we all have to stand to fight this 
malaise. 
Madam, we have been debating this issue for the last two days. 
Some Members said that there was a security lapse and some others said that 
there was no security lapse. I don't want to go into that controversy. But one 
thing comes across my mind and the question that I have asked myself so 
often, ever since that incident happened on 13 th December, is: Could we have 
saved them? Could we have saved those lives? Let us not forget the fact that 
when the terrorists came our Watch an d Ward Staff was without arms. They 
were only armed with their courage; they were only armed with their 
patriotism; they were only armed with  their line of duty; and they became 
victims of that dastardly attack. The onl y thing that I keep on asking myself is: 
Could we have avoided it? The issue is not whether there was security lapse 
inside the Parliament or not. The same  question arises and it has arisen 
several times in my mind even in respect of Kargil. When I think of the fact that 
more than 500 people of our country sacrif iced their lives in the interest of the 
nation, again, the question keeps on ha unting me: Could their lives have been 
saved? The answer is "Yes, those lives could have been saved". Those lives 
could have been saved, if we had kept a vigil. Those lives could have been 
saved, if, as a polity, we were most  sensitiye to the concept of national 
security. If I were to say the words that I am going to say now, people might 
think that I am being partisan. I will quote the words of a person who wrote the 
Kargil Report, Shri K. Subrahmania m, when he talked about the national 
security. This is what he said and I quote: 
"There is a reluctance both on the part of the politicians and the 
bureaucrats to devote time and effort for this purpose. It is 
considered adequate, if people are briefed when the need arises. 
Starting preparations to counter a thre at after it is materialised is the 
surest way of inviting disaster." 
We are starting to counter a threat after it has already materialised. 
We salute those who laid down their lives with courage. But we must 
introspect. Not the Government alone, we as a nation must introspect. Have 
we in the last decade or so taken note of the concerns of national

[19 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA

outside the gates of Parliament also - some sort of scanning - so that we can

SHRI AHMADUDDIN AHMAD KHAN (DURRU) (Rajasthan): Madam 
Deputy Chairman, I have just a few clarific ations to seek. At the very outset, I 
wish to join my colleagues in condemning this act of terrorism and all acts of 
terrorism in this country; and also pay my homage to the martyrs. Madam, 
through you, I want to seek certain clar ifications from the Home Minister. At a 
function held by the Pioneer, the Prime Minister had said, "This was very well 
planned at the heart of the nation; and at the Parliament." But I noticed the 
very next day, the Commissioner of Police saying, "The terrorists have first 
gone to the airport and finding that it was very well guarded, then, they came 
here." So, I think there is a bit of cont radiction at the top level. I would be 
grateful if the hon. Home Minister clarifies this point. 
The other thing which I would like to  mention is about a report that 
appeared in the newspaper two days  back that the car dealer who had 
voluntarily and immediately gone to t he police with the photographs and the 
documents was held in custody for four days, and that his family was not 
allowed to see him and his lawyers were not allowed to see him. This was the 
report two days back. If this kind of treat ment is meted out nobody is going to 
come forth in the near future and give voluntary information to the police.  I 
would appreciate a comment on this. 
The third clarification that I would like to seek is on the article written 
by our colleague, Shri Kuldip Nayyar on the I4 m December wherein he 
mentioned that the Watch and Ward staff to ld him during this period that there 
was a proposal to give them arms, but it had been lying with the Home Ministry 
for a long time. Now, is there any such proposal? If there is such a proposal, 
what is its position? 
Lastly, I would like to say that a solution to terrorism is not only a law 
and order problem, is not only a military problem but is also a political problem. 
I would request the Government to kindly consider the political option also. 
Thank you very much.
