WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Agricultural research and extension system 
*21. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH : Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have made any assessment of the health of 
agricultural research and extension system and its ability to cope up with the 
challenges that Indian agriculture faces; and 
(b) if so, what are the findings thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) Yes Sir. (b) 
The details are given in the statement. 
2 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
National Agricultural Research System 
The assessment of Research & Extension System is an on-going process 
and in-built mechanism in the system, both at Micro and Macro level. 
The agricultural research being done by the Institutes, National Bureaux, 
National Research Centres, Project Di rectorates and All India Coordinated 
Research Projects is periodically assessed at micro level by Quinquennial Review 
Team, Research Advisory Committee, St aff Research Council and Scientific 
Panels. On these Committees/Teams the eminent external subject- matter experts 
are nominated. 
The Macro level assessment is made periodically by eight Subject Matter 
Divisions functioning at Indian Council of Agricultural Research Headquarter, 
New Delhi; Director's Conference involving all the Directors of National 
Agriculture Research System; Vice-Ch ancellor's conference of all State 
Agricultural Universities; Project Co ordinators' Meeting and Steering Group 
& Working Group constitued by Planning Commission. 
As per the findings of these review mechanisms and the Steering/Working 
Group constituted by Planning Commission, the system has the capability 
enough to cope with the challenges faced by Indian Agriculture. As 
demonstrated in the past, the National Agricultural Research System has the 
potential, the ability and the will to make Indian agriculture most resilient and 
dynamic. 
1. In the post-independence period, the technolgoy back-up by the 
agricultural scientists coupled with positive policy support, and dedicated 
work of farmer have contributed  to the phenomenal increase in 
agricultural, animal and fish production in India. The Green, Blue, White 
and Yellow Revolutions bear testimony to the success of this strategy. 
We have been able to produce a record harvest of 209 million tonnes of 
food grains during 1999-2000. There has been a four-fold increase in the 
production of wheat, three-fold in rice, maize and cotton and two -fold in 
sugarcane, sorghum and oilseeds. The production of fruits and vegetables 
tripled during last fifty years. Meat production enhanced by six-fold and 
fish by seven-fold. The country became one of the largest milk producer 
and second in production of wheat, rice, onion, fruits & vegetables and 
sugarcane. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2002] 
2. Apart from production, the total factor productivity grew at more than 
1% per annum over the last 25 years. 
3. The total agricultural exports, which were to the tune of Rs. 17496 crore 
during 1995-96 increased to Rs.28909 crore during 2000-2001. 
4. Another important indicator of the health and viability is its willingness to 
evaluate its weaknesses and equip itself. 
In the past, the Indian Agriculture has faced many challenges. From a 
food deficit State, the country became self-sufficient in food grain production. 
Now, the challenges before the Indian agriculture are: Doubling food production 
in current decade; increasing cropping intensity and productivity; Developing 
technology for arid agriculture and horticulture; Addressing second generation 
problem in Green Revolution areas; Sustaining the health of soil and other 
natural resources; Addressing the cost and quality issues; Development of 
farming modules suitable for small and marginal farmers; Gearing up the system 
to face WTO Regime and Globalisati on; and Maintaining standards of 
excellence and ethics in the performan ce of personnel to provide space for 
creativity and research. 
In order to keep pace with emerging needs, the research priorities have 
been changing. So as to address these issues, the ICAR is providing due thrust 
to the following areas: 
• Farming system approach 
• Fillip to diversification to floriculture and horticulture 
• Organic farming 
• Conservation of natural resources and bio-diversity 
• Post-production technologies and surplus management, particularly in 
milk, fruits and flowers 
• Market driven production models 
• Training of Scientists in sun-rise sectors 
• Continuous efforts to develop human resource to enhance its quality in 
general and in terms of values and ethics in particular 
• Focussed attention and specific efforts in far flung areas like NE Region, 
Andman & Nicobar for givng support to those dimensions of agriculture 
4 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
suitable to these areas i.e. floriculture for North East and fisheries for 
Andman & Nicobar 
• Greater emphasis on research on pulses and oilseeds 
• Setting up mechanisms for obtaining market intelligence to align 
production and research strategies 
• Demand driven transfer of technology 
The system is aiming at consolidating the gains of the Green Revolution 
by laying emphasis on sustainability of agriculture, restoration of health of 
soil, addressing the problems of erosion and water depletion, and converting 
'Grey Areas' into 'Green'. 
Findings of The Steering Committee on Agriculture & Allied Sectors for 
X Five Year Plan, Constituted by Planning Commission under the Chairmanship 
of Prof. M. S. Swaminathan 
• The ICAR-SAUs research system has contributed significantly to the 
Indian Agriculture in terms of varieties/material and production 
technologies. 
• The country became one of the largest milk producer in the World. 
• We are second in production of Wheat, Rice, Onion, Fruits & Vegetables 
and Sugarcane. 
• Efforts to be made for consolidation and not proliferation of agricultural 
Institutes and effective Zero base Budgeting should be done. 
• There should be adequate synergy between the user of research and 
research activities of ICAR-SAUs system. 
• Laid stress on conversion of "Green Revolution" into an "Evergreen 
Revolution" without associated ecological or social harm. 
• Advocated the need to match production and post- harvest technologies. 
• Revitalization of research tempo to obtain major break through in hybrid 
technology for Rice. 
• Establishment of Eco-regional S&T consortia comprising SAUs, ICAR 
Institutions and Rural and Women's Universities. 
• Setting up of a UGC type organisation for SAUs and the organisation of a 
India International Centre for Agricultural Research and Education. 
 
5 
 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2002] 
• Setting of an "Agricultural Science Commission" to study the proliferation 
ofSAUs. 
• Research priorities suggested are: 
• Conservation and enhancement of ecological foundation of farming viz., 
land, water, bio-diversity, forest, oceans and the atmosphere. 
• Organisation of Multi-disciplinary Monsoon and Climate Management 
Centres in different agro-climatic zones. 
• Dry farming through appropriate land use and water conservation 
measures. 
• Special attention to hill areas, coastal regions, islands, J&K and North 
East Region. 
• Diversification of cropping and fanning systems and greater attention to 
crop livestock integration. 
• Intensification of research on under utilised crops 
• Intensification of research on sustainable captive culture fisheries. 
• Mainstream ing gender consideration in agriculture research and curricula. 
Findings of X Plan Working Group on Agricultural Research and 
Education constituted by Planning commission 
• Biotechnological approach to be extended to crops, animals, fisheries and 
m icro-orgasnisms. 
• Inclusion of International Agriculture as part of education. 
• Strengthening of monitoring evaluation and impact assessment. 
• Addressing problems of integrated rural development in a holistic manner. 
• Close linkages with other Universities and IITs. 
• KVKs may be transferred to States and DAC. 
Extension System   - 
Though the Agriculture being a State subject, the extension programmes 
are being implemented by respective St ates as well as Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research (ICAR) throgh its network of Krishi Vigyan Kendras 
(KVKs). The Division of Agricultural Extension of the ICAR and Department 
6 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
of Agriculture and Cooperation periodically assess the refinement and 
dissemination of technology projects. 
An Assessment of Extension System was made at the time of formulation 
of National Agricultural Technology Project (N ATP-1995-96) funded by World 
Bank. The findings indicated that the Training & Visit (T&V) System of 
Extension operated in major States over two decades was found to be suited for 
dissemination of crop production practices, however lacked Farming System 
Approach and participatory methods and did not address to the diversification 
needs of the farmers, Research - Exte nsion-Farmer linkage remained weak. T 
& V System did not influence the technology dissemination in rainfed areas. 
To  address these issues and to bridge these gaps the Department of 
Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) launched a project on pilot basis 
at 70 centres viz. Technology Assessment and Refinement through Institution 
Village Linkage Programme (I VLP) and 40 Agricultural Technology Information 
Centres (ATIC). 
The Department of Agriculture and Cooperation has also taken up 
"Innovations in Technology Dissemination Component", under World Bank 
funded National Agricultural Techno logy Project. The project is being 
implemented in 7 States viz. Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, 
Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Orissa and Pu njab by establishing an Agricultural 
Technology Management Agency (ATMA). The ATMA has built in mechanisrh 
for assessment of gaps in the existing extension system through Farmers' 
Participatory Methodology and Development of Strategy to fill in these gaps 
by creation of a district level "Strateg ic Research and Extension Plan". The 
initial results obtained through various modes show that it has been showing 
encouraging results in terms of following milestones: 
• Adopting group approach to extension 
• Adopting bottom up planning procedures for setting location specific 
research and extension agenda. 
• Making the technology dissemination farmer driven and farmer 
accountable 
• Enabling public private partnership in technology dissemination 
• Moving towards integrated broad based extension delivery 
• Improving research-extension-farmer linkages 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2002] 
• Enhancing application of IT for effective connectivity and technology 
dissemination 
• Moving towards sustainability of extension services 
• Convergence of line department programmes and operating Government 
support through ATMA in gap filling mode 
• Providing marketing extension linkages

*31. SHRI MAN MOHAN SAMAL: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) Whether it is a fact that environmental hazards in the Talcher-Angul 
region of Orissa are a serious cause of concern; 
(b) whether Government have studied the impact of industrialization on 
environment in that region; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [1March, 2002] 
(d) the measures taken to control environmental crisis in the region during 
the last three years? 
THEMINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) Talcher-Angul region of Orissa has been identified as one of the 24 
environmental problem areas in the country. 
(b) to (d) Brief details of steps taken to mitigate the environmental impacts 
and to control environmental degradation in the area are given in the Statement 
below. 
Statement 
Steps taken to mitigate the environmental impacts and to control 
environmental degradation in Talcher-Angul region of Orissa. 
1. The Talcher-Angul region was studied in-depth and an environmental 
action plan prepared in 1990. This included implementation of specific 
pollution control measures by various industries located in the region 
such as National Aluminium Company Limited, National Thermal Power 
Corporation and Mahanadi Coalfields Limited. 
2. The pollution control status of the area was reviewed by Central Pollution 
Control Board in 1995. Further, the environmental status was studied by 
Central Pollution Control Board through Orissa State Pollution Control 
Board and a status report was prepared in 2000. The study has inter-alia 
indicated that the water quality of Brahamani river as well as the ambient 
air quality in the region have improved. 
3. Various measures have been taken to mitigate the environmental hazards 
of industrialization including mandatory environmental clearance under 
the provisions of Environmental Impact Assessment Notification, 1994, 
environmental monitoring of the industries and implementation of unit-
wise pollution control schemes such as 100% recycling of the ash pond 
over flow and augmentation of Electrostatic Precipitators in the Thermal 
Power plants, installation of waste water treatment facilities in the coal 
mines and provision of drinking water facilities to the affected villages.

Losses of Steel Industry 
*38.    SHRI GAYA SINGH: 
SHRI J.CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the indigenous steel industry is in a great crisis and 
almost all the units are running under losses; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons for the present crisis; 
(c) whether the steel industry is demanding ban on import of seconds and 
defective steel; and 
(d) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI BRAJ 
KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) and (b) Due to adverse conditions in the steel market, both 
domestic and international, the Indian steel industry is parsing through a difficult 
phase. Although many steel plants are maintaining a healthy record of operating profits, 
they are posting net losses after accounting for depreciation and interest. The primary 
factors responsible for this situation are (i) excess supply and low demand for steel in 
the domestic market, (ii) import of steel at low prices, (iii) falling steel prices, (iv) high 
production costs, (v) closure of important export markets for the Indian steel due to 
protectionist measures initiated by a number of importing countries, (vi) general slow 
down in the Indian economy and recessionary trends in the global steel market. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The main steel producers have been demanding a ban on the 
imports of seconds and defectives. To cope with the problem of cheap imports of 
seconds and defective steel items, the following steps have been taken by the 
Government: 
•    Floor prices on imports of seconds  and defective of certain steel items 
imposed earlier continue; 
32 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
• Restrictions have been imposed on entry of seconds and defectives 
through a few designated ports only; 
• An additional duty of 10% has been imposed on the import of seconds 
variety of HR Coils; 
• Pre-shipment inspection certification has been made mandatory for 
imports of seconds and defectives of all steel items; and 
• Budget for 2002-2003 has proposed certain steps to further reduce 
import of seconds and defectives.

THEMINISTEROFENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. BAALU): (a)

Statement-1 
Steps taken by the Government to combat wildlife trafficking are: 
(1) Steps taken at the State level: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting and 
commercial exploitation under the provisions of the Wildlife (Protection) 
Act, 1972. 
(ii) State level and District level coordination committees have been set up in 
several States to prevent poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(2) Steps taken at National level: 
(i) Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional Offices for wildlife 
preservation in major export and trade centres of the country to prevent 
smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(ii) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute wildlife offenders. 
(iii) Financial and technical help is provided to the States under various Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tigar, Project Elephant, Development of 
National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-development around Protected Areas 
for enhancing the capacity and infrastructure of the States for providing 
effective protection to wild animals. Items supported in the schemes include 
creation of 'Strike Forces', providing arms, mobiles and communication 
facilities to the protection staff and rewards to the informers. 
(iv) A Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set up under the 
chairmanship of Secretary, Envi ronment & Forest, Government of 
India, for control of poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(v) Export of wild animals and their derivatives is prohibited under EXIM policy. 
(vi) Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments to lend a 
helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching and illegal trade in

Pollution in Yamuna between Wazirabad and Okhla 
203. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
75 
 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2002] 
(a) whether it is a fact that Delhi is the fourth most polluted city in the 
world and the river Yamuna bed between Wazirabad and Okhla is having most 
polluted stretch; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what immediate and stringent measures are being taken to check and 
improve the pollution standard in the city? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) and (b) The ranking of Delhi as the fourth most polluted city in the world was 
based on the levels of suspended particulate matter. This ranking was not relating 
to water pollution. The stretch of river Yamuna between Wazirabad and Okhla in 
Delhi is polluted due to the following reasons: 
(i)      Discharge of untreated or partially treated domestic and industrial 
waste into Yamuna due to shortage of treatment capacity. 
(ii)    Siltation and collapse of nearly 91 km. trunk sewer system out of 
the total 131 km. 
(iii)   Problems of unsewered areas and slums from where the waste 
water is directly discharged into the drains leading to river 
Yamuna. 
(iv)      Lack of dilution capacity in the river. 
(c) The following measures are being undertaken by the Government of 
Delhi to improve the water quality of river Yamuna in Delhi: 
(i)     Desilting and rehabilitation of trunk sewers. 
(ii)       Replacement of under-sized sewers. 
(iii) Augmentation of Sewage treatment capcity of about 725 million 
gallons per day and rehabilitation/repair of ancillary works such as 
sewage pumping stations, rising mains and trunk sewers etc. 
(iv) Upgradation of existing sewage treatment plants to better paramenters 
of Biological Oxygen Demand of 10 milligram per litre, suspended 
solids of 15 milligram per litre and coliforms to less than 1000 
Most Probable Number per 100 millilitre. 
(v) Subject to technical feasibility, providing sewerage facilities in the 
remaining 165 out of 567 unauthorised/regularised colonies, 43 of 
135 urban villages and 4 out of 44 resettlement colonies and thereby 
covering all the unauthorised/regularised colonies and urban villages. 
76 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) Construction of about 1000 additional community toilet complexes 
in unsewered areas under Yamuna Action Plan. 
(vii) Completion of 15 no. of common effluent treatment plants to ensure 
that all the industries treat their effluent so as to meet the prescribed 
standards. Unauthosied industries operating in various parts of 
Delhi without proper arrangement of pollution control to be shifted 
or closed. 
(viii) Removal/relocation of Jhuggis from the Yamuna River banks and 
drains. 
(ix) The existing sewerage network to be appropriately maintained using 
three tier maintenance schedule i.e. prevention,  routine and 
breakdown maintenance instead of only breakdown maintenance 
prevalent at present. 
(x) Interception and diversion of municipal waste water flowing through 
19 drains into Delhi stretch of the river and conveyance of this 
waste water to the sewage treatment plants. 
(xi) Maintenance of minimum flow of water in the stretch between 
Wazirabad and Okhla.

Restriction on Production and Sale of Bt Cotton 
206. SHRI BRAHMAKUMAR BHATT: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are restrictions on Bt Cotton and on production and sale 
of its seeds; 
(b) whether Government or any Government agency has issued any 
instructions to cotton producing States for destroying or not cultivating Bt 
Cotton and.for not producing Bt Cotton seeds; 
(c) whether any State is giving conditional permission for research or for 
any such purpose; and 
(d) whether such cotton is being cultivated in China, America and some 
other countries, without any kind of restriction? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Bt cotton is a bollworm resi stant genetically modified crop. As 
per Rule 7 of the Rules for Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and storage of 
hazardous microorganisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms of Cells 1989 
notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, no persons can import, 
export, transport, manufacture, pr ocess, use or sell any hazardous 
microorganisms or genetically engineered organisms or cells without the 
approval of the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) set up in the 
Ministry of Environment and Forests. GEAC has so far not accorded approval 
for commercial release of Bt cotton in  the country. The Maharashtra Hybrid 
Seed Company (MAHYCO) has been in volved in the research, development 
and testing of transgenic Bt cotton varieties. The large scale field trials of 
MAHYCO's Bt cotton are under way. 
(b) Navbharat Seeds Pvt. Ltd, Ahmedabad has marketed seeds of a 
transgenic Bt cotton variety (Navbharat 151) in Gujarat without any biosafety 
assessment and the mandatroy approval of GEAC, thereby violating the 
provisions of 1989 Rules and the Environment Protection Act 1986 the 
GEAC has directed the Gujarat State Biotechnology Coordination Committee 
to: 
• procure the cotton bolls of Navharat 151 crop from the farmers at the 
appropriate support price; 
• separate the lint and seed; 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2002] 
• destroy the seed and store the lint in safe custody till farther orders 
from GEAC; 
• complete destruction of crop residue by uprooting and burning and 
sanitation of fields. 
This company is undertaking seed production of transgenic cotton in 
Nandyal and Kumool districts of Andhra Pradesh. The Government of Andhra 
Pradesh has been directed to take nece ssary action for stopping the transgenic 
seed production and multiplication programme of the Navbharat Company, on 
the lines of the directives given to the Government of Gujarat. 
(c) State Governments do not accord approvals for research on genetically 
modified crops. Research activities including small scale field trials of genetically 
modified crops are approved by the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation 
set up in the Department of Biotechnology under the 1989 rules, approvals for 
large seale field trials and commercial release of genetically modified crops are 
given by the GEAC. 
(d) Bt cotton is registered for cultivation in United States of America, 
China and Australia after approval by the competent authorities.

† 222. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the schemes formulated by Government for strengthening financial position 
of women of the country, particularly rural women, by providing employment 
opportunities and preventing exploitation against them; and 
(b) the details of necessary action taken by Government for effective 
implementation of these schemes? 
THE MINISTEROF STATE IN THE MTNISTRYOF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) The details of the 
schemes are given in the statement (See below). 
(b) The Department is regularly monitoring the implementation of the schemes 
through periodic progress reports, review meetings, visits and inspections and

Statement 
Women specific Schemes of Department of Women and Children 
1. Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women (STEP) 
This Programme launched in 1987, seeks to provide updated skills and new 
knowledge to poor and assetless women in the traditional sectors, such as, agriculture, 
animal husbandry, dairying, fisheries, handlooms, handicrafts, khadi 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
92 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
and village industries, sericulture, soci al forestry and wasteland development 
for enhancing their productivity and income generation. This would enhance 
and broaden their employm ent opportunities, including self-employment and 
development of entrepreneurial skills. Women beneficiaries are organised into 
viable and cohesive groups or co-operatives. A comprehensive package of 
services, such as, extension, inputs, ma rket linkages etc. are provided besides 
linkage with credit for transfer of assets. 
2. Women's Economic Programme (NORAD) 
This programme was launched in 1982-83 with assistance from Norwegian 
Agency for Development Cooperation (NORAD). Under this programme, 
financial assistance is given to Women's Development Corporations, Public 
Sector Corporations, autonomous bodies, and voluntary organisations, to train 
poor women, mostly in non-traditional trades and to ensure their employment in 
these areas. Some of the trades are computer programming, electronics, watch 
assembling, radio and television repairs, garment making, secretarial practices, 
community health work, embroidery, weaving, etc. Financial assistance is given 
to the grantee organisation for hiring of training-cum -production sheds, training 
costs, machinery and equipment, stipend to the trainees and remuneration for 
the trainers. 
3. Condensed Course of Education for Adult Women 
The Scheme of Condensed Course of Education for Women was started 
by the Central Social Welfare Board during the year 1958 with the objective of 
providing basic education and skills to needy women and also to benefit 
widows, destitute deserted women and also those belonging to economically 
backward classes. Under the Scheme, grant is given to voluntary organisations 
for conducting courses of two-year duration for preparing candidates for primary, 
middle and matric level examinations and one-year duration for matric failed 
candidates. 
4. Vocational Training Programme 
Based on the national policy on skill development for girls and women 
the Central Social Welfare Board had started the Scheme of the Vocational 
Training Programme in the year 1975 to train women in marketable trades and 
also to upgrade their sk ills in order to enable and empower them to access 
remunerative employment opportunities, which will enhance their self-confidence 
and self-esteem. The Training Programme is organised in rural, tribal, backward, 
urban slum areas through Voluntary organisations in the traditional and non- 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2002] 
traditional trades like Computer Training, Community Health Workers, 
Paramedical Vocations, Typing and Shorthand, to enable them to get employment in 
Government, Public Sector Undertakings, Corporations, Autonomous Bodies, Private 
Sector etc. Special emphasis is also laid on implementing this Programme in After 
Care-Homes, Women Cell of Jails and other custodian institutions. The organisations 
are identified through State Social Welfare Advisory Boards in all States/U.Ts. And 
implementation of the training programme is monitored through field machinery. The 
skills of traditional artisans are also being upgraded to provide opportunities for 
self-employment. The Scheme has been instrumental in providing job opportunities 
to a large number of needy women and thereby enhancing their socio-economic 
status. 
5. Awareness Generation Projects for Rural & Poor Women 
The Awareness Generation Programme aims to identify the needs of rural and 
poor women and to generate awareness among them about their status in the family 
and society and to activate mem to work for achieving their rights and to deal with 
social issues. Since 1993-94, special emphasis has been given to participation of 
women in Panchayati Raj institutions and their role in promoting national integration 
and communal harmony. Some of the schemes of the Department of Women & 
Child Development such as the Rashtriya Manila Kosh and the Manila Samridhi 
Yojana have also been included in mis Scheme to motivate rural women towards 
self-reliance. Relevant topics are taken up in a camp of 8 days duration for 25 
beneficiaries, which are followed by 2 days for detailed evaluation of the camp. The 
assessment of the impact of the camp on the beneficiaries and the community is 
done within 6 months on completion of the camp. A sum of Rs. 10,000/- is given to 
an organisation for one Awareness Generation Project. Training of organisers is a 
pre-requisite condition for organising the camps for which a number of training 
centres in every state have been identified by the National Standing Committee and 
CSWB. The expense of Rs. 1000/- per trainee is provided by the Central Social 
Welfare Board. 
6. Socio- economic Programme 
The Socio-Economic Programme of th e Central Social Welfare Board 
endeavors to provide employment opportunities on full or part time basis to 
destitute women, widows, deserted and the physically handicapped, to 
supplement their meager family income. Besides, women entrepreneurs are 
encouraged to exhibit and sell their income. Besides, women entrepreneurs are 
encouraged to exhibit and sell their products through Exhibition-cum-Melas 
94 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
organised by State Boards at Distt. level. The Central Social Welfare has two different 
types of schemes of assistance under this Programme as follows: 
• Agro - based Units 
The Central Social Welfare Board assists voluntary organisatons for setting up agro-
based units like dairy, poultry, piggery, goatery etc. for poor and needy women. 
However, for the past few years' proposals for Agro-based Units were not 
considered. 
• Production Units 
Voluntary organisations are encouraged to set up Production Units, which can 
provide employment on full or part time basis to women. Project proposals should 
be cleared by District Industrial Centres, KVICs etc. who look into viability of the 
projects. A gram is provided by the Central Social Welfare Board to facilitate 
setting up a Production Unit by the grantee institution. 
7. Education Work for Prevention of Atrocities on Women 
The scheme of assistance to voluntary organizations for Education Work for 
Prevention of Atrocities on Women was started in 1982. Under this scheme, universities, 
colleges, women studies centres, institutions of higher learning and voluntary 
organisations are given financial assistance for undertaking various activities such as 
production and publication of the educative journals, articles, books, conducting 
surveys and studies on violence against women, awards to best films, short plays, short 
stories, etc., translation of such material from one language to another language, 
holding seminars, conferences, meetings, exhibitions, film festivals etc. holding of 
training camps for social workers including Govt functionaries, legal literacy 
camps/para legal training camps, use of traditional media such as street plays, 
puppetry etc. organising Women Development Centres in educational institutes and legal 
and counselling services to women prisoners etc. 
8. Rural Women's Development and EmpowemeMt Project (Swa-Shakti) 
The Swa-Shakti Project, earlier known as Rural Women's Development and 
Empowerment Project, was sanctioned on 16-10-1998 as a Centrally-sponsored 
Project for a period of 5 years with an estimated outlay of Rs. 186.21 crore. In addition, an 
amount of Rs.5 crore is being provided during the project period, for facilitating the 
setting up, in the project states, of Revolving Funds for giving interest-bearing loans to 
beneficiary groups primarily during their initial formative stage. 
95 

RAJYA SABHA [ 1 March, 2002] 
9. Integrated Women's Empowerment Programme (Swayamsidha) 
Swayamsidha is an Integrated scheme for women's empowerment. It is based 
on formation of women into Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and aims at holistic 
empowerment of women through awareness generation, economic empowerment and 
convergence of various schemes. 
The vision of Swayamsidha is to mobilize and develop empowered women 
who will: 
• Demand their rights from family, community and government; 
• Have increased access to, and control over, material, social and political 
resources; 
• Have enhanced awareness and improved skills ; and 
• Be able to raise issues of common concern through mobilization and 
networking. 
As a result of Swyamsidha, the nature of changes envisaged are expected to result 
in self-reliant and sustainable institutions, which priorities women's needs and interests 
and bring about their social and economic empowerment. These institutions should 
be ready in the last year to take over the role of implementers to ensure complete 
sustainability of the approach even after completion of Swyamsidha. 
10. Women in Difficult Circumstances (Swadhar) 
The scheme has been designed with a flexible and innovative approach to 
cater to the requirement of various types of women in distress in diverse situations 
under different conditions. The scheme provides shelter, counselling and training 
for women in difficult circumstances who do not have any social and economic 
support. 
11. Rashtriya Mahila Kosh 
The National Credit Fund for Women (Rashtriya Mahila Kosh) was set up on 
30th March, 1993 with corpus fund of Rs.31 crores with the major objective of meeting 
the credit needs of poor women, particularly in the informal sector. 
The RMK set up under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 is managed by a 
Governing Board comprising 16 members. The Minister of State for Women and Child 
Development is the Chairperson of the Kosh. Besides extending micro 
96 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
finance, RMK has also launched a scheme to support the formation and 
stabilization of Women's Self help Groups (SHGs). Under this scheme, RMK gives an 
interest free loan upto Rs. One lakh for formation and stabilization of 25 SHGs. The loan is 
convertible into grant on fulfillment of certain conditions. 
Women Specific Schemes of other Ministries/Departments 
Ministry of Rural Development 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) 
The scheme of Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) came into force 
with effect from 1.4.1999. Under this programme, the erstwhile programmes viz. Integrated 
Rural Development Programme (IRDP), Training of Rural Youth for Self Employment 
(TRYSEM), Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), Supply of 
Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITA), Ganga Kalyan Yojana (GKY) and Millions 
Well Scheme (MWC) were integrated. This is a holistic programme covering all aspects of 
self-employment such as organisation of the poor into self-help groups, training, credit, 
technology and infrastructure. SGSY has a provision of covering 40% women 
beneficiaries as Swamrojgaries. The scheme mainly aims to bring the assisted poor families 
(Swarozgaris) above the poverty line in three years by providing them income 
generating assets through a mix of bank credit and Government subsidy. This 
programme is implemented through DRDA and with the active involvement of 
Panchayati Raj institutions, banks the line departments and the NGOs. 
Ministry of Labour 
1. Women's Vocational Training Programme 
Launched in 1977, National Vocational Training Institute (NVTI) for Women was set 
up at NOIDA; and Regional Vocational Training Institutes for Women (RVTIs) have 
been set up at Mumbai, Bangalore, Trivandmm, Hissar, Calcutta, Tura and Munnar, for 
offering skill training facilities to women so as to enable them find employment in 
industry as semi-skilled/skilled labourers; or instructors in vocational institutes; or 
engage in income generating activities/self -employment. Four new Regional 
Vocational Training Institutes for Women are also being set up with Work Bank 
assistance at Indore, Vadodara, Jaipur and Allahabad. 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2002] 
2. Grant-in-aid to the State Government 
(i) Establishment of new ITIs for Women; and 
(ii) Strengthening of new Women's ITIs. 
The scheme aims to expand the Women's Vocational Training Programme both 
quantitatively and qualitatively, to meet the growing skilled and semiskilled man 
power requirement for Industry/Service sector/domestic income generating industries 
and self employment. The scheme targets to expand the skill training facilities for 
women and to make the women employable in the industry as semi-skilled worker. 
3. Vocational Rehabilitation of Women with Disabilities 
The scheme aims to coordinate with various Govemment and non-
government organisations to promote speedy rehabilitation of the disabled women by 
providing training, job and self-employment services. Vocational Rehabilitation Centres for 
Handicapped, under the Govemment of India, Ministry of Labour are at 17 places. VRC 
at Vadodara is exclusively for women and the other Centres assist both men and 
women with disabilities. 
Ministry of Science and Technology 
I. Science and Technology for Women 
The main objectives of the scheme are to promote research, development and 
adaptation of technology to improve the life, working conditions and opportunities of 
gainful employment of women, especially in rural areas, and to increase the contribution of 
women to science and technology and development. 
Primary Education in Rural Areas 
† 223. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of education policies made so far since independence of the country, 
alongwith the recommendations made under the said policies, for imparting 
elementary education to all the children of rural areas; 
(b) the details of necessary action taken by Govemment for implementing 
the said recommendations;    
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
98 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) to what extent Government have achieved success in this regard; and 
(d) the present policy of Government with regard to imparting elementary 
education to all the children of age group of 6-14 years of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT PR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) The Directive Principles of the 
Constitution of India under Article 45 envisaged provision of free and compulsory 
education to all children up to the age of 14 years. 
Following the above Constitutional di rective, the Na tional Policy on 
Education, 1968 stated that strenuous efforts should be made for the early fulfillment 
of the Directive Principle under Article 45 of the Constitution seeking to provide free and 
compulsory education for all children up to the age of 14. Suitable programmes should 
be developed to reduce the prevailing wastage and stagnation in schools and to ensure 
that every child who is enrolled in school successfully completes the prescribed 
course. 
The National Policy on Education (NPE-1986), as revised in 1992, also 
reiterated that free and compulsory education of satisfactory quality should be provided 
to all children up to 14 years of age before we enter the Twenty-first Century. 
(b) and (c) In pursuance of the above policies, the Government of India had 
launched a number of programmes/schemes like Operation Blackboard, Teacher 
Education, Non-formal Education, Mahila Samakhya, National Programme for 
Nutritional Support for Prinamry Education, District Primary Education Programme 
and State Specific Projects such as Lok Jumbish and Shikha Karmi Project in Rajasthan, 
Bihar Education Project (BEP) in Bihar and Basic Education Programme in Uttar 
Pradesh. 
As a result, considerable progress has been achieved towards universal 
isation of elementary education. During the period 1950-51 to 1999-2000, the number 
of primary schools has increased by more than 3 times from 2.10 lakh in 1950-51 to 
6.42 lakh in 1999-2000 whereas the number of upper primary shcools increased 15 
times from 13,600 in 1950-51 to 1,98,000 in 1999-2000 
The enrolment at primary stage has increased by 5.91 times between 1950-51 and 
1999-2000, and for girls the increase was 9.16 times. At the upper primary level, the 
increase in enrolment during this period was more than 13 times, and in the case of girls 
the increase was about 33 times. The average annual growth 
99 

RAJYA SABHA {1 March, 2002] 
rates of enrolment at primary and upper primary levels were 1.73 per cent and 2.54 per 
cent respectively during the period 1950-51 and 1999-2000 
(d) The Constitution (Ninety-Third Amendment) Bill, 2001 was passed by the Lok 
Sabha on 28-11 -2001. The Bill provides for free and compulsory education for all children in 
the age group 6-14 as a Fundamental Right. 
The Government has also launched the Scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) 
in November, 2000 to pursue universal elementary education in a mission mode. 
The goals of SSA are as follows:- 
vii)    All 6-14 age children in shcool/EGS centre/bridge course by 2003, 
viii)    All 6-14 age children complete five year primary education by 2007 and 
ix)    All 6-14 age children complete eight years of schooling by 2010. 
x)    Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis on 
education for life; 
xi)    Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 2007 and at 
elementary education level by 2010; 
xii)    Universal retention 2010. 
This Ministry has also constituted National Level Mission under the 
Chairmanship of the Prime Minister vide Resolution dated 2.1.2001.

Statement 
Guild of Service, a voluntary organisation, had organised a Conference 
'Capacity Building of Marginalised Women: Widows' in New Delhi during 1 st to 3rd 
February, 2002. 
In the conference, among other things, factors contributing to multiple and 
very often hidden human rights violation of widows in South Asian countries and need 
for properly interpreting and understanding religious texts and scriptures which 
calls for respect for women were discussed. The Conference adopted a declaration 
calling for abolition of customs, practices and traditions that discriminate against 
women through legal reforms, action against those who violate the physical, social 
and human dignity of widows, reviewing laws to ensure widows get their just share 
of inheritance and mainstream ing widows through social security and economic 
empowerment schemes. 
The Government has taken a number of steps that covers the 
recommendations and are for the rehabilitation the marginalised women, especially those 
living in Vrindavan and adjoining areas. These include: 
• Constitution of a Central Committee headed by the Minister of State for 
Women & Child Development to inter-alia, chalk out a strategy for 
rehabilitation of the marginalised women; 
• Government has launched a new scheme for rehabilitation of women in 
difficult circumstances, called ‘Swadhar’ under which two projects have been 
considered for Uttar Pradesh; 
• Government is implementing schemes such as. Setting up of 
Employment-cum-Income Generating Units for Women (NORAD), 
Support to Training and Employment Programme (STEP), Socio-
Economic Programme (SEP), Condensed Courses of Educational and 
Vocational Training for Women (CCE& VT) under which preference is given 
to such marginalized women in the matter of providing assistance.

is provided for implementing self employment programmes through

Old Age Pension Schemes and the Social Defence Schemes provide for 
pension and rehabilitation of such marginalised women; 
• The State Government of U.P. has also established two shelter houses 
and provided necessary arrangements of medical care and protection 
of the inmates living in these shelter houses.

Sexual exploitation of Children 
263. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has endorsed Global Commitment (Declaration) adopted 
in Yokohama for action at national, regional and international level to eradicate 
commercial, sexual exploitation of childen; 
(b) the number of countries which have pledged to adopt this commitment 
(Declaration); 
(c) whether a permanent machinery has been constituted to oversee its 
implementation; and 
(d) if so, what are the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) and 
(b) 138 countries, including India, sent deligations to the Yokohama conference 
organised by four NGOs and UNICEF. The conference adopted the Yokohama 
Global Commitment which included an Explanation Statement by India. In that 
Statement it was made clear that reference to extra-territorial criminal laws in the 
said Commitment is intended to ensure that the offender is tried in the country in 
whose jurisdiction the offence is committed; if he can not be so tried by virtue of 
his being not present in that country and his being not extradited for facing trial, 
138 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
he is tried in the country of which he is a national or in the country of which he 
is a habitual resident or in the country where he is present. Reservations have

States. 
(c) and (d) Safeguards against trafficking exist in our Constitution, The 
Indian Penal code and The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956. On the basis 
of these, the Government of India had formulated a National Plan of Action to 
Combat Commercial Sexual Exploitation of Women and Children in 1998, after 
extensive consultations. The implementation of the Plan of Action is supervised 
and monitored by a Central Advisory Committee at the Central level. Similarly 
the States/UTs have set up State Advisory Committees for this purpose. These 
facts were highlighted at the Yokohama World Congress.

1. Divisional Railways Users' Consultative Committee (DRUCC).

L Provision of amenities in the area with which the Committee is

them for consideration by the Zonal Railway Users' Consultative

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI O. 
RAJAGOPAL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Anti-Collision Devices (ACDs) are microprocessor based 
communication devices, fitted on locomotives, brake vans and located in stations 
and level crossings. These give distinct identification to the locomotives and brake vans 
and using the global positioning system and angular deviation count principle, detect 
"collision like" situations and initiate application of brakes in the locomotives in a 
range of 3 kms. The ACDs also help in detecting train partings and initiate warning 
signals at level crossings. Field trials of ACDs are being undertaken. The ACDs will 
be considered for provision on Indian Railways on satisfactory performance during the 
trials and availability of funds.

approximately.

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow 
to the tragic and untimely demise of Shri G.M.C. Balayogi, Speaker, 
Lok Sabha, on the 3 rd March, 2002 in a helicopter crash in Kaikalur, 
West Godavari District, Andhra Pradesh, at the age of 51. A promising 
career has, thus, been cut short at the unkind hands of destiny. 
Born in October 1951 at Yedurulanka in East Godavari District 
of Andhra Pradesh, Shri Balayogi wa s associated with several social 
and cultural organisations and took special interest in the upliftment of 
the poor and the downtrodden sections of the society.. 
Shri Balayogi started his career with the Vice-Chairmanship of 
the Cooperative Town Bank of Kakinada in 1986. Thereafter, he 
became Chairman, Zila Praja Parishad, East Godavari District, in 
1987, in which post he continued till 1991. He was elected as a 
Member of the Tenth Lok Sabha in 1991. He was elected to the 
Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assemb ly in 1996 and remained as its 
Member till 1998. He also served as the Minister of Higher Education 
in the Andhra Pradesh Government and took the initiative in 
streamlining and reforming the educational system. In 1998, he was 
again elected as a Member of the Twelfth Lok Sabha and was elected 
as the Speaker, Lok Sabha, in March, 1998. In 1999, he was re-
elected to the Thirteenth Lok Sabha for the third time and was elected 
as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha for the second time in October, 1999 
and continued to hold office till his death. 
In his capacity as Speaker, he was Chairman of the Business 
Advisory Committee, Rules Committee. General Purposes Committee 
of the Lok Sabha and Presiding Officer of the Legislative Bodies in 
India. He was also President of the Indian Parliamentary Group, the 
National Group of Inter-Parliamentary Union and the India Branch of 
the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2002] 
He  led the  Indian  Parliamentary Delegations to the  Ninety-
ninth, Hundredth and Hundred-and -first Inter-Parliamentary Union 
Conferences and the Forty-fourth and Forty-fifth Commonwealth 
Parliamentary Conferences. He also led several Parliamentary 
Delegations to various countries. 
He adorned the high office of the Speaker at a young age and 
conducted the proceedings of the Lok Sabha smoothly and efficiently. 
As the Presiding Officer of the House, he ensured that all sections of 
the House got equal opportunity to participate in the proceedings of 
the House in a fair and orderly manner. He stood for norms and 
ethical values. At his initiative, in a Conference of the Chief Ministers, 
Presiding Officers and Leaders of various political parties in 
Parliament and State Legislatures, a Code of Conduct to be observed 
by Members of Parliament and State Legislatures was adopted. Soft 
spoken and mild mannered, he endeared himself to one and all, and 
showed firmness, when needed. 
In the passing away of Shri G.M.C. Balayogi, the country has 
lost a young and dynamic parliamentarian. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as 
a mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.)

deep sympathy,
